articles.title: U.S. Investigates Deadly Strike on Wedding in Iran, Vance Says
articles.body:
The U.S. is investigating a strike on a wedding in southern Iran, Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday, as reports suggest American weapons killed at least five people and injured dozens of others.
“We’re investigating it because obviously we care,” Vance told reporters. “We want to know.”
The strike represents the U.S.’s latest controversial action in its war with Iran, raising questions about its conduct and civilian harm. Washington and Tehran have escalated their attacks this week, ending a lull in hostilities since July.
But Vance said he was “extremely skeptical” about reports coming from Iranian state media, arguing they have “not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far.”
Iranian state media reported that a residential building in Kuhestak was attacked on Tuesday evening, where a wedding was being celebrated. Among the casualties was a 4-year-old kid. Reuters and the New York Times independently verified footage from the scene and found that a wedding was taking place when the building was struck.
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that it “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”—and responded to a broader barrage of American attacks by launching missiles and drones at sites used by the U.S. in Middle East states. The Iranian Red Crescent Society, a humanitarian group, also urged a probe from the International Criminal Court to assess potential violations of international law.
The U.S. Central Command said Wednesday it was already looking into reports of the incident but argued that the “U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps],” referring to Iran’s armed forces branch.
Vance also defended U.S. military action, telling reporters: “If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran: when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.”
What we know about the strike
On the evening of Sept. 1, CENTCOM reported strikes on military targets, including “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Iranian media later reported four deaths and at least 68 injured in Kuhestak, a coastal town on the Strait of Hormuz, where trade has been bottlenecked since the start of the U.S.-Iran war in late February. The strikes happened at around 9:30 p.m. local time, per the Red Crescent.
Analyses of footage from the incident conducted by Reuters and the New York Times reveal that wedding guests were gathered in a Kuhestak building. Amid the celebration, what was likely a U.S. munition hit the building and, as the Times put it, “brought down the roof.”
Experts told Reuters and the Times that weapon fragments seen in Iranian media were consistent with what Americans have used.
The attacks on Kuhestak also hit a communications tower roughly 100 m away from the building. A human rights group told the Associated Press that one of the four people initially reported killed—a 16-year-old—was struck by shrapnel near the tower rather than at the wedding. Iranian state television said Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had since died in hospital following the strike, bringing the reported death toll to five.
Axios reported that CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike.
Civilian casualties raise concern
The Red Crescent sent a letter to the International Criminal Court Wednesday calling for “an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” citing the “civilian character” of the strike’s location.
The organization also argued that under the Rome Statute, intentionally directing attacks on civilians and knowingly launching a clearly excessive attack may constitute “war crimes.” However, both Iran and the U.S. are nonparties to the Rome Statute, so the ICC does not have automatic jurisdiction over them.
Still, “the laws of war state that civilians are protected from military attacks,” Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “A wedding is not a military objective, particularly in a civilian residential building. It is clear that there was a direct missile hit to the home. This would render the attack unlawful.”
It’s also not the U.S.’s first involvement in strikes that hit civilian structures without obvious military use and that endangered or killed civilians. On the first day of the war with Iran on Feb. 28, a U.S. Tomahawk missile hit a primary school in Minab—just 30 km (18 mi) away from Kuhestak—where more than 100 children were killed.
O’Brien, however, says she is skeptical about any result from the U.S.-led investigation of the wedding strike: “The U.S. track record is to only investigate when allegations gain significant public traction, and even when any convictions occur, the penalties are minor or pardons are given.”

articles.title: Iran launches missiles toward Jordan, ‘powerful explosion’ reported
articles.body:
Lebanese media reported Friday evening that two people were killed in a new wave of Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon, while Iran launched ballistic missiles toward Jordan in a separate escalation that produced interceptions visible from northern Israel.
According to Lebanese reports, two people riding a motorcycle were killed in a strike in the village of Roumine. Other targets were reportedly struck in the Nabatieh area and Al-Fawqa. Shortly afterward, people spending time around the Sea of Galilee filmed interceptions in the sky.
The IDF said the interceptions were taking place over Jordan but appeared from northern Israel to be directly overhead.
Iranian media initially reported a “powerful explosion in Jordan.” Iran’s Fars News Agency and the Saudi outlet Al Hadath later reported that missiles had been fired toward a U.S. base in the kingdom.
The Israeli strikes in Lebanon come as contacts with the Lebanese government continue.
Only a day earlier, five prisoners were released and returned to Lebanon.
At the same time, Lebanese authorities are searching for the remains of former leaders of the country’s Jewish community who were abducted and murdered by terrorist organizations during the 1980s.
Operation on Ali Taher Ridge
The latest strikes in Lebanon also come against the backdrop of the IDF’s operation on the Ali Taher Ridge, a strategic Hezbollah stronghold in southern Lebanon.
On Thursday, after Reuters reported that Iran had threatened to “respond forcefully” to Israeli activity on the ridge, the IDF released details of the operation and its objectives. Israeli security officials said that although IDF troops had trapped dozens of Hezbollah terrorists inside the complex, there was no basis for Iran’s claim that members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had also been caught there.
Israeli troops identified openings through which Hezbollah terrorists could escape from the underground complex, placed them under surveillance and prevented attempts by the organization to assist those trapped inside from the outside.
Hezbollah initially tried to transfer equipment to its men, but security officials said the difficulty increased as the operation continued, creating pressure inside the organization.
During the fighting, Israeli forces positioned around the exits exchanged fire with Hezbollah terrorists attempting to escape and killed dozens, according to the IDF. The military said troops established operational control through ambushes, fire on tunnel shafts, grenades, drones and other strikes.
Although Iranian officials have continued to claim that dozens of Iranians and Lebanese remain trapped there, the IDF said Thursday that the clearing of Hezbollah’s underground infrastructure on Ali Taher Ridge had been completed and that all terrorists inside had either been killed or escaped.
“The operation to neutralize the underground infrastructure that was cleared of terrorists is continuing, and once it is completed, the IDF will redeploy in a renewed defensive posture,” the military said.
According to the IDF, the underground complex contained command centers, weapons rooms, generator rooms, living quarters, showers and a kitchen, allowing Hezbollah forces to conduct combat operations and remain underground for extended periods.
The military described it as “strategic infrastructure built over two decades, financed and planned by the Iranian terror regime.”
First published: 20:06, 09.04.26

articles.title: Analyst ties drone surge to CIA chief’s Moscow warning
articles.body:
- CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on August 25 and 26 to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member, as Russian drones repeatedly entered Romanian airspace that month.
- Moldova closed at least three border crossings in August due to nearby drone strikes, including one around its August 27 Independence Day.
Civilians and infrastructure on NATO’s eastern flank faced near-daily Russian drone incidents through August, even as the CIA director made a rare visit to Moscow to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member state, according to Cristian Vlas, an Eastern Europe analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED).
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on August 25 and 26 for meetings with Russian intelligence officials, a trip first reported by the Wall Street Journal and CBS News, which said Ratcliffe’s goal was to discourage Russia from testing NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense commitment. President Donald Trump later called the visit “semi-routine.” The Kremlin confirmed contacts took place but said Ratcliffe did not meet with President Vladimir Putin.
Romania recorded repeated Russian drone incursions into its airspace through August, according to Vlas, most of which Romanian and NATO aircraft intercepted. Drone debris landed in both uninhabited and residential areas along Romania’s southeastern coast, near Black Sea tourist sites and oil infrastructure, he said.
On August 20, a Romanian Air Force F-16 destroyed a drone laden with explosives roughly 80 nautical miles (148 kilometers) off Constanța, near the Neptun Deep gas platform operated by OMV Petrom and Romgaz, after a commercial ship spotted the device drifting toward the site, according to Romania’s Defence Ministry. Ukraine’s military told Romanian officials the drone was not one of theirs; Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia, though authorities have not formally identified who built it.
Vlas said Moldova has also been affected by spillover from Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory near its border, with at least three crossing points temporarily closed during August because of nearby drone strikes. A Russian strike on August 21 damaged the Tabaky crossing, and a Ukrainian border crossing near Vulkaneshty-Vinogradovka closed on August 25, two days before Moldova marked its Independence Day on August 27.
“Moldova has also been affected by the spillovers from Russian attacks on Ukrainian grain routes, with three border checkpoints having been closed temporarily amid daily drone incidents, including on its Independence Day, highlighting Chisinau’s air defense vulnerability,” Vlas said.
Vlas said the recurring drone incidents are straining air defense resources across Eastern Europe, and that they may be compounding “possibly renewed Russian-linked sabotage attempts” in Germany, Estonia and Slovakia, which he said could be intended to divert investigative and prosecutorial resources while testing European Union resolve to continue backing Ukraine.
“Calling these increasingly regular security incidents hybrid warfare threats undermines efforts to define the deteriorating security environment, develop EU-wide and local solutions, and call out Russia’s systematic use of openly military or covert violence against Europe,” Vlas said.

articles.title: Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
articles.body:
Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
Kyiv • UNN
Systematic strikes complicated logistics, weakened air defenses, and caused disruptions to energy and fuel supplies in Crimea. The 2026 holiday season has effectively been ruined.
Systematic strikes by the Defense Forces of Ukraine against the energy, fuel, transport, and military infrastructure of occupied Crimea throughout the spring and summer have significantly complicated Russia’s use of the peninsula as a military hub. Operation "Crimean Switch off" did not lead to the immediate collapse of the Russian grouping or the energy system of occupied Crimea, but it has had a cumulative effect: problems with logistics and fuel supplies, power outages, and reduced air defense capabilities. A collateral but tangible consequence was the effective disruption of the holiday season, on which a significant share of local small businesses depends. UNN discussed the consequences of the systematic Ukrainian strikes on facilities in the occupied peninsula with experts.
"Crimean Switch off": what kind of operation is it?
"Crimean Switch off" is the name of a campaign by the Unmanned Systems Forces aimed primarily at energy infrastructure in the occupied territories. It is being conducted in parallel with Operation "MoLoChKa," whose targets include tankers and other vessels providing Russian logistics in the Black and Azov Seas.
"Crimean Switch off" began on July 1, while "MoLoChKa" began on July 6. Both special operations fit into Kyiv’s strategy of coercing Russia into peace.
One of the first targets of Ukraine’s middle strikes was the "TES-Terminal-1" terminal in Kerch. It is a large facility for storing light petroleum products. Substations with voltages of 110–220 kV in Yalta, Kerch, Sudak, Feodosia, Alushta, and other populated areas were systematically targeted.
According to the Unmanned Systems Forces, by August 28, 315 energy facilities had been hit since the start of the operation. The targets included the Balaklava Thermal Power Plant in Sevastopol and gas-turbine stations in Karierne and Naumivka.
In parallel, Ukraine carried out strikes against maritime logistics. As of August 22, according to the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, 242 vessels in the Black and Azov Seas had been hit. It was separately reported that four of the five key ferries of the Kerch crossing had been disabled.
The Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the main strikes on tankers using attack UAVs manufactured by FirePoint
In addition, at the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian troops destroyed the main bridges connecting the peninsula with mainland Ukraine, which significantly complicated logistics for Russian occupation forces.
How strikes on Crimea affect the front
For Russia, Crimea remains primarily a major military and logistical hub through which, among other things, the occupying forces in southern Ukraine are supplied. That is why strikes by the Ukrainian military are not limited to the energy sector.
According to military expert Ivan Stupak, this summer Ukraine has been systematically targeting air defense, electronic warfare systems, warehouses, bases, fuel infrastructure, and Russian logistics.
This is important because Crimea is not simply territory for Russia, but a major military hub. And Ukraine is precisely trying to gradually undermine its capabilities. This concerns strikes on warehouses, bases, logistics, fuel infrastructure, and other military infrastructure. The goal here is absolutely clear—to reduce Russia’s ability to supply its grouping in southern Ukraine. In particular, this concerns Zaporizhzhia Oblast—the areas of Huliaipole, Orikhiv, and Stepnohirsk. We are trying to create conditions for Russia under which it will be more difficult for it to support its offensive operations
According to him, the fight against Russian road logistics has become a separate area.
And I would say that we have already significantly undermined their capabilities in Crimea. Over the past three months, according to the data I have seen and that can be verified, Ukraine has destroyed about 600 trucks every month. These are very large figures. In fact, this represents a serious reduction in the volumes that Russia can transport and supply
However, this does not yet mean the destruction of the entire Russian supply system on the southern front. Military expert Mykhailo Zhyrokhov draws attention to the key role of the Crimean Bridge and railway connections.
As long as such an important strategic structure as the Crimean Bridge exists, Russia has the ability to maintain more or less normal supplies for the troops stationed on the occupied peninsula. We understand that a single train can deliver more fuel than dozens of fuel trucks, which can then be destroyed on the road from Novorossiysk. Rail supply is the foundation
At the same time, experts identify the gradual weakening of Russian air defenses on the occupied peninsula as one of the most noticeable results of the Ukrainian campaign.
“Madyar” showed strikes by Ukrainian UAVs of the Fire Point company against Russian air defense systems
If we are talking specifically about military capabilities, I would say that Russia’s air defense capabilities have been severely undermined. Almost every day, reports emerged that either a radar station, an anti-aircraft missile system, or even some aircraft at an airfield had been destroyed. This is gradually reducing the Russians’ ability to shoot down our drones
But in his view, this is not yet a strategic turning point in this area.
Stupak also does not expect an immediate effect from the Crimean operations. In his assessment, this is rather a cumulative effect and a gradual reduction in the capabilities of Russia’s military machine in Crimea.
If this trend continues in the autumn and winter, I would not speak of some immediate collapse of Crimea. I am more inclined toward a different scenario - Russia may gradually reduce its presence on the peninsula
In his view, the Russians could potentially move some administrative and military structures to the mainland, change their basing locations, and reduce their use of airfields in Crimea.
Such a reduction in presence is quite likely. I think that Ukraine could potentially further reduce Crimea’s importance by 20–30%. And this, accordingly, could reduce the Russians’ ability to use the peninsula to launch attacks on Ukraine’s southern regions
Strikes on energy infrastructure: disruptions are already occurring, but the system is holding for now
Energy infrastructure became a separate area of the operation. Systematic attacks on substations, generation facilities, fuel terminals, and oil depots have caused disruptions both to civilian infrastructure and to the occupying forces. According to Zhirokhov, prolonged power outages in Crimea were reported in Russia.
Then a campaign of strikes on Crimea’s energy infrastructure began. What did this lead to? To certain shifts. Reports appeared on Russian public channels that individual districts had been left without electricity for one, two, or three days at a time
According to Zhirokhov, the key factor enabling Russia to compensate for some of its losses remains the energy bridge between Crimea and Krasnodar Krai.
Along with the construction of the Crimean Bridge, the Russians built what is known as an energy bridge, through which they transmit electricity from Krasnodar Krai. Therefore, without destroying this energy bridge, all these strikes are, you know, for now merely figures in the General Staff’s reports: so many electrical substations hit, some other facilities hit. This certainly creates problems, but it does not break the system
At the same time, fuel problems arising from strikes on tankers and oil depots could directly affect Russian units at the front. According to Stupak, internal Russian reports recorded a reduction in fuel supplies.
One separate and important issue is fuel and energy infrastructure. Strikes on oil depots, fuel terminals, and other facilities create problems for the Russians. I saw their internal reports and their response to Ukrainian strikes. At certain points, they acknowledged a reduction in fuel supplies to the front by approximately 20–25%
In modern warfare, fuel is needed not only for armored vehicles and automobiles, but also to operate generators, on which, among other things, the ability to charge FPV drone batteries, maintain communications, and so on depends.
And at certain moments, the Russians complained that they were short of fuel for their generators by approximately 20%. This means they have to conserve their batteries and launch fewer reconnaissance and strike drones. But I cannot say that this is already a widespread problem along the entire front line. Nevertheless, the local problems are noticeable
The situation in Crimea may become even more complicated in winter. Economist and former spokesperson for NJSC "Naftogaz of Ukraine" in the Lviv region Viktor Halchynskyi predicts problems with supplying the peninsula with gas as well.
If the gas issue is further addressed, it will be cold in Crimea. As far as I know, the storage facilities located there have also been damaged. If the Defense Forces take certain further actions, combined with the shortage of liquid fuel and electricity, this could lead to an extremely uncomfortable winter on the peninsula, even taking into account the fact that the climate there is warmer
Resort season under attack: Crimea has lost tourists and money
The disruption of the resort season was the most tangible consequence for the civilian population of occupied Crimea. Problems with fuel and electricity, constant strikes, disruptions to transport logistics, and the overall danger made vacationing in occupied Crimea almost impossible. At the end of June, Russians who had come to vacation on the occupied peninsula fled en masse. Even 15-kilometre queues to leave Crimea were recorded.
According to Halchynskyi's estimate, the 2026 resort season became the worst for the occupied peninsula since 2014.
It is difficult to assess the damage in absolute figures because we can see the situation in the temporarily occupied territory exclusively through media estimates and reports that leak onto the internet from individual users. But we can say with confidence that the damage from the 2026 resort season, which in fact did not take place, is probably the greatest since the occupation, that is, since 2014
In his opinion, the actual disruption of the resort season became the culmination of a process that began immediately after the occupation of Crimea, when Ukrainian and European tourists stopped visiting the peninsula.
Due to the lack of fuel and electricity, constant air attacks, and the blocking of transport connections, the season had effectively ended prematurely in June. Accordingly, the tourism sector failed to receive substantial funds
According to experts, the consequences are being felt primarily by local small businesses, whose earnings had been tied to the summer for decades. Mykhailo Zhyrokhov notes that the model was simple: the money earned in summer enabled many Crimeans to live through the rest of the year.
But psychologically and socially, this is undoubtedly a major blow for the residents of Crimea. Most small businesses in Crimea—both under Ukraine and under Russia—were built specifically around the resort season. People earned money in summer and then effectively lived on it in autumn and winter. Now this model has been disrupted. Certain economic problems have arisen, and people have failed to earn the expected amount of money
Halchynskyi also speaks of the gradual winding down of businesses and the possible outflow of the economically active population from the peninsula.
If we are talking about business in Crimea, it is obvious that a very large number of people earned their living specifically from tourism. Now businesses are closing. There are problems with energy and problems with security. And, judging indirectly from what we see, this process has gradually begun
According to him, there is no mass evacuation at present, but people may move their economic activity outside Crimea or leave the peninsula altogether.
At the same time, experts remind us that Crimea has always received subsidies from the state budget. For the occupation administration, a decline in tourist flows also means reduced revenues and greater dependence on Russia's federal budget.
Most likely, the Crimean authorities will once again have to appeal to Russia's federal budget and request more direct transfers for 2027. Crimea is already the most heavily subsidized region, and the reduction in tourist flows only increases this dependence
This, in his view, is one of the additional effects of the Ukrainian campaign of strikes on Crimea. After all, any additional Russian budget expenditures on Crimea reduce the possibilities for military spending.
It is beneficial for us if money from the Russian budget is spent not on military purposes. If Russia is forced to direct more funds toward supporting Crimea, compensating for losses in the tourism sector, restoring infrastructure, and making direct transfers, this already works to our advantage. Because Russia never has an excess of money. And the more the Russian budget is forced to spend on problems arising from Ukrainian strikes, the fewer resources potentially remain for the war
At the same time, Zhirokhov believes that losses suffered by small businesses due to the disrupted resort season will not be a problem for the Russian authorities, since the Kremlin will not consider the interests of Crimeans a priority.
Thus, the main effect of Ukrainian operations in Crimea lies in the gradual increase in the cost of occupying Crimea for Russia. Moscow is forced to simultaneously compensate for losses to military logistics, restore energy facilities, strengthen air defenses, support the subsidized economy of the peninsula, and respond to Crimea's growing unattractiveness to tourists.
And if the systematic nature of such strikes is maintained, occupied Crimea will become increasingly difficult to use simultaneously as a military bridgehead, a logistics center, and a symbolic "showcase" for Russians.

articles.title: ‘I Wouldn’t Call it a War’: Vance Downplays Conflict With Iran, Even as Strikes Continue
articles.body:
Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday that he would not characterize the United States as being at war with Iran, even as the two countries have exchanged strikes in recent days and the Trump Administration has declined to say when a conflict now stretching beyond six months might finally end.
“I wouldn’t call it a war,” Vance told reporters at a White House press briefing, the first since Karoline Leavitt stepped down as press secretary last month. “Right now, there is no active shooting.”
The distinction was striking after a renewed burst of hostilities this week, including American strikes inside Iran and Iranian attacks in the region. But it echoed an argument that President Trump and other Republicans made in the earliest days of the conflict: that the United States was carrying out a limited military operation rather than embarking on another prolonged Middle Eastern war, which, under the Constitution, would require congressional approval.
More than six months later, that distinction has become increasingly difficult to sustain. The United States has repeatedly bombed targets inside Iran as Tehran attacks commercial shipping vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to higher energy prices.
Vance acknowledged what he called a recent “flare-up” but argued that the most intensive phase of the American campaign had ended long ago. “Major combat operations are currently not ongoing, and they haven’t been ongoing in a very long time,” he said.
He said Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale campaign that followed last year’s Operation Midnight Hammer, lasted roughly six weeks. The earlier operation, he said, destroyed Iranian nuclear facilities, while Epic Fury severely damaged Iran’s conventional military and its ability to produce weapons and rebuild its nuclear program.
But Vance offered little indication of when the broader confrontation might end, saying the Administration would not commit itself to a timeline while Iran continued threatening commercial shipping and global energy supplies. Asked whether the conflict would be over before November’s midterm elections, Vance said he did not know. “You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said, adding: “When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?”
The answer underscored the open-ended nature of a conflict that Trump and others in the Administration repeatedly predicted would be brief. As recently as Wednesday, the President said he did not believe it would last “much longer.” But his Administration is simultaneously intensifying economic pressure on Iran, maintaining a naval blockade, and reserving the option of further military strikes if Iran attacks American interests or interferes with commercial shipping.
History of avoiding the word “war”
Presidents have long resisted the “war” label in conflicts undertaken without a formal declaration of war. Harry Truman called the American intervention in Korea a United Nations “police action,” while Bill Clinton avoided describing NATO’s bombing campaign in Kosovo as a war. Barack Obama similarly argued that the 2011 intervention in Libya did not constitute a “war” requiring congressional authorization.
In March, Trump openly acknowledged that referring to the conflict as “war” carried legal significance because Congress had not authorized it. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say, if you use the word war, that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” he told House Republicans at the time. “They don’t like the word ‘war,’ because you’re supposed to get approval, so I’ll use the word ‘military operation,’ which is really what it is.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson similarly insisted shortly after the initial strikes that the country was “not at war,” describing the campaign instead as “a very specific, clear mission.” Democrats have rejected that characterization and repeatedly tried to force votes requiring congressional authorization for continued hostilities. Those efforts have failed largely along party lines. The dispute has revived a decades-old argument over presidential war powers and the extent to which a president can sustain military operations abroad without explicit approval from Congress.
Economic and military pressure
Vance said Thursday that the administration would not rely on Iran to negotiate in good faith and would instead use whatever tools it considered necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and to protect global energy markets.
He argued that Iran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was “effectively gone” and that oil traffic through the crucial waterway was nearing its pre-conflict level. Shipping data, however, shows traffic remains well below where it stood before the fighting began. The Administration has made restoring commercial traffic through the strait a central objective as energy prices have become an increasing political liability ahead of the midterms.
Vance acknowledged the pain of higher gasoline prices but argued that they could have risen substantially more without American intervention in Iran. “Gas, frankly, could have been much, much higher were it not for our efforts,” he said. He declined to predict when prices might return to around $3 a gallon, saying the more important objective was ensuring “that Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon.”
The Administration is now pursuing what amounts to a strategy of intermittent military force combined with sustained economic pressure. Last week, it announced “Operation Economic Outcast,” an effort to further isolate Iran from its remaining trading partners. But the campaign has so far produced limited results, and imposing sanctions aggressive enough to cripple Iranian trade could require confronting countries including China, India, and Russia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that the Administration expected the principal pressure on Iran going forward to be economic, while reserving the right to use military force when necessary.
Iranian uprising
Trump himself has resumed publicly encouraged Iranians to challenge the regime, writing on Truth Social on Tuesday, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”
When asked by TIME on Thursday whether the Trump Administration was considering arming Iranian dissidents or providing them with other direct assistance, Vance declined to provide more details. “Everything that could happen is on the table: economic pressure, military pressure, diplomatic pressure, covert pressure,” he said. “Of course, these are tools in the President's toolkit.”
Iranian leaders, meanwhile, have shown little sign of capitulating. Its leadership remains divided between officials advocating negotiations and hard-liners pressing for confrontation, and Tehran has continued striking American interests and allies in response to U.S. attacks.
The renewed American bombing has also brought fresh scrutiny of civilian casualties. Iranian authorities said a U.S. strike this week hit a wedding celebration in Sirik in southern Iran, killing at least five people and wounding scores more, including women and children. A New York Times visual analysis and a weapons expert concluded that the wedding was struck by a bomb released by American forces during attacks in the area.
Vance said the episode was under investigation but expressed deep skepticism about Iran’s account. “The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” he said. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
“Obviously, sometimes things happen,” he added. “When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them, so we’re investigating it very fully.”

articles.title: Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
Damascus - Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani met with Israel’s Mossad chief Roman Gofman in Jordan on 23 August following days of escalating tensions that resulted in an Israeli strike on a Syrian airbase in northern Idlib.
According to reports, the two met in order to “lower the temperature” following this latest bout of tensions.
Whilst it was not the first round of direct diplomacy between Syrian and Israeli officials, it represented the first instance of direct meetings at such a senior level.
The renewed risk of escalation comes amid growing competition between Israel and Turkey, as each regional power pursues a different - largely incongruous - strategy over Syria’s future.
Yet US efforts to restrain Israeli aggression have achieved some limited success, say analysts.
Growing competition
Israel claimed the strike on Abu al-Duhur airbase on 18 August was due to Turkey being close to breaching “the status quo on security matters” by deploying troops into Syria. Turkey denied that any of its forces had been at the base before or during the attack,
The airstrike was “clearly a message not just to the Syrian administration but also to Turkey,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at The Soufan Centre, told The New Arab.
“They want Turkey to know that they have the ability to strike them anywhere in Syria in order to deter further perceived encroachment.”
According to Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation, Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), this follows a pattern of behaviour in which Israel strikes any military installation that Turkey seeks to redevelop.
“They also struck T4, Hama and Palmyra airbases following Turkish attempts to redevelop them,” he explained to The New Arab. “It serves a dual purpose of limiting Turkish influence within Syria and preventing the Syrian military from redeveloping.”
This comes amid what Rose describes as “a growing competition” between Turkey and Israel regionally.
Turkish-Israeli relations have soured massively since 7 October. Whilst both countries have full diplomatic relations, Turkey recalled its ambassador in November 2023 in protest over Israeli actions in Gaza.
In February, meanwhile, former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett described Turkey as belonging to a “monstrous axis,” alongside Qatar, in part for its hosting of Hamas officials.
A recent article in Israel Hayom, a pro-Likud outlet, assessed the possibility of an Israeli strike on Turkish forces in Syria triggering NATO’s self-defence clause. It concluded that such an attack would not draw in Turkey’s NATO allies.
Turkey recently signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan - what some commentators have taken to calling an ‘Islamic NATO.’
“The mutual defence agreement is a major step,” Issam Al-Reis, a researcher with ETANA, a Syrian research group, told The New Arab.
“For Saudi Arabia, it is a counter to a possible Iranian attack, and for Turkey it is important to deter a possible future scenario in which it's attacked by Israel,” he added.
“There is a sense of increased recklessness from the Israelis and Turkey is likely wondering if after Iran, they are next on the hit list.”
Divided strategies
Part of the tensions are driven by Israel and Turkey’s conflicting strategies in Syria. “Turkey was one of the primary supporters of the Syrian revolution,” says Al-Reis.
“Now their strategy is driven by a desire for a stable Syria that will allow the millions of refugees within Turkey to return home and provide a calm southern border.”
As such, they have sought to develop Syria’s state capacity, and “expand its military footprint in order to stabilise the country and counter groups that they consider to be terrorist organisations like the Syrian Democratic Forces,” explains Al-Reis.
Yet Al-Abdullah cautions about wholly conflating Israel’s attempts to counter Turkey with its own strategy within Syria. “These two dynamics are linked but also separate,” he argues. Israel has its reasons to oppose the Syrian government.
It sees “a Syria capable of launching attacks as a threat and so wants to see Syria weak and fragmented,” believes Rose. “They seek to counter or at the very least delay Syrian rearmament.”
Similarly, Israel has supported non-state actors within Syria, such as Druze Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri’s National Guard in Suweida, in order to keep Damascus weak.
The US, seeking a stable centralised Syria, has been attempting to restrain Israel with mixed results. US Special Envoy for Syria, Tom Barrack, condemned Israel’s recent strike as “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”.
However, Al-Abdullah notes that according to ACLED’s data, the number of Israeli strikes on Syria is consistently decreasing over time, but that “occasionally Israel still decides to act without the US greenlight”.
Stalled talks
Syrian and Israeli officials have taken part in several rounds of talks in Paris, the latest being on 6 January 2026, designed to establish a ‘deconfliction mechanism’ and set out the ground for the possible future security architecture between the two countries.
According to analysts, these talks have been largely inconclusive and have failed to halt Israeli violations both within the newly occupied territories in Quneitra and Daraa and beyond.
On 14 August, following the resumption of Syrian air force training flights, Israel had reportedly planned on striking a number of airbases in order to disable the last vestiges of Syria’s air force.
It is worth noting that 80% of Assad’s air force was destroyed by Israel in the days following the fall of the Assad regime, leaving Syria now with barely a handful of old Soviet fighter jets.
Whilst the planned strikes were reportedly blocked by the White House, the days after saw numerous attempts to resolve the dispute - including a reported phone call between Shaibani and Gofman - which failed to prevent escalation.
Part of the reasoning behind the recent meeting in Jordan is likely to correct this, with both sides discussing the possibility of establishing “a special operations room” in Jordan under US supervision to prevent any confrontation in Syria.
“This meeting is significant both because Syria’s senior leadership actually met with the Israelis but also because it was publicly acknowledged by the Syrians,” says Al-Abdullah.
This represents a step change in Syrian officials' willingness to candidly acknowledge their attempts to foster dialogue with Israel. Despite that, he remains pessimistic about the outcome of talks.
“The two actors are negotiating different things,” he explains. Syria is hoping to return to a status quo ante, which would see Israel leave the newly occupied areas in return for a deconfliction arrangement similar to the 1974 deconfliction arrangement.
Whereas Israel, reflecting a new post-7 October security mindset that is also visible in Lebanon and Gaza, wants to create “an unliveable buffer zone close to their borders through demolitions, eviction and the poisoning of agriculture”.
Ultimately, this would entail Israel leveraging its position to pressure Syria into accepting major concessions like diplomatic normalisation or the recognition of Israel’s 1981 annexation of the Golan Heights - both of which are political non-starters in Damascus.
It is for this reason that he expects this pattern of latent tensions that sporadically erupt to continue.
However, Al-Abdullah stresses that despite the fierce rhetoric on all sides, neither side is seeking a full-blown conflict and so for now “whilst Syria might be a theatre for confrontation, it is not yet the Middle East’s next battleground”.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Advanced enemy technology failed to shield aircraft from indigenous air defenses
articles.body:
Advanced enemy technology failed to shield aircraft from indigenous air defenses
TEHRAN — Iran’s air defense commander says the country’s recent experience of war has demonstrated that technological superiority alone cannot guarantee the safety of an attacking force, stating that Iranian forces developed and upgraded new domestically produced air defense systems even as the fighting was underway.
Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, commander of Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defense Headquarters and the Army’s Air Defense Force, made the remarks on Friday.
Elhami said Iran had relied on “100-percent Iranian capabilities” during the recent conflict, identifying courageous leadership, national cohesion and public support as three of the principal pillars of the country’s wartime resilience.
He said Iranian defense personnel had developed and manufactured air defense systems during the conflict, subsequently deploying them to operational areas where, according to his account, they were used against hostile aircraft.
“Advanced enemy technology did not provide them with immunity,” Elhami said, arguing that even highly sophisticated aircraft entering the battlefield could not be assured of a safe return.
His comments were consistent with a report published Friday by Tasnim, which said Iran’s Army air defense force had achieved self-sufficiency in supplying the weapons, equipment and defense systems it requires by relying on domestic expertise, knowledge-based companies and universities.
Elhami said the Iranian air defense industry was increasingly drawing on young defense scientists, domestic technology companies, universities and operational experience accumulated during the war.
He also warned that, in Iran’s assessment, the conflict was not necessarily over and that the armed forces needed to remain prepared for 'new threats and fronts.'
US and Israel failed to achieve objectives
Separately, Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia, spokesman for Iran’s Army, said the United States and Israel had failed to achieve the objectives they had pursued during their latest military campaign against Iran.
Speaking at an event in Mashhad on Friday, Akraminia said the adversary had entered the conflict after making a series of miscalculations about Iran, including its society, military capabilities and political structure.
He added that the attackers had sought to degrade Iran’s missile and nuclear capabilities, overthrow its government and ultimately partition the country. “None of these objectives was achieved,” he said.
Akraminia also cited 'a failure by the United States and its Western allies' to build a broader military coalition against Iran.
He said the confrontation had become a test of political and national will as much as military capability, arguing that Iran’s religious beliefs, social resilience and experience from previous conflicts had strengthened its ability to withstand pressure.
Iran announces further strikes on US bases
Against that backdrop, Iran’s Army said it had continued its missile and drone operations against US military positions in the region.
In a statement, the Army said Iranian forces had struck satellite communications systems, equipment storage facilities and fighter aircraft shelters at Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait.
The Iranian military also said missile and one-way attack drone strikes had targeted troop positions and radar systems at Al Minhad Air Base in the United Arab Emirates.
Iran said the attacks caused damage to communications infrastructure and aircraft shelters.
The two bases are important components of the US military presence in the Persian Gulf. Ahmad al-Jaber is a significant US air facility in Kuwait, while Al Minhad has served as an important hub for air operations and the movement of foreign forces in the region.

articles.title: Iran strike leaves U.S. Navy with a serious supply problem
articles.body:
- The Navy has about 20 ships and 20,000 personnel in the Middle East, resupplying at sea every five to six days since Iran struck its Bahrain logistics base on February 28.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln spent most of nine months deployed without a port call before docking in Thailand this week en route to San Diego.
The U.S. Navy is running open-ended combat deployments in the Middle East without access to most of its regional supply bases, forcing ships to resupply at sea roughly every five to six days rather than pulling into port, The New York Times reported.
Iran struck the Navy’s logistics hub in Bahrain on February 28, the first day of the current war, according to the Times. Other regional ports large enough to handle an aircraft carrier or a supply ship remain within range of Iranian missiles and drones, making them effectively off-limits.
With nearby bases unavailable, Navy supply ships now sail 2,200 miles to Diego Garcia, a small island in the Indian Ocean, to load food, fuel and other goods before returning to the fleet. The next-closest option is Singapore, 3,700 miles away, a route that requires passing through the Strait of Malacca, one of the world’s busiest commercial shipping corridors.
The Navy currently has about 20 ships and 20,000 sailors and Marines deployed in the Middle East, according to the Times. That includes two aircraft carriers, the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) and the USS George Washington (CVN 73), along with 12 destroyers carrying roughly 3,700 personnel combined, and a three-ship amphibious ready group carrying about 5,000 Marines and sailors. Keeping that force fed and fueled requires more than 420,000 meals and about 8 million gallons of fuel every week, the Times reported. A single carrier’s air wing alone burns roughly 2 million gallons of fuel weekly, even though the ship itself is nuclear-powered.
Resupply at sea requires the receiving ship and the supply ship to sail together on identical course and speed, often for hours, while staying within roughly 150 feet of each other despite wind, waves and current. Sailors fire lines across to the other vessel using rifles, then connect the ships with steel cables that carry fuel lines and pallets of supplies. Helicopters simultaneously ferry additional pallets of food, spare parts and mail between the ships in slung cargo nets.
These deployments have no fixed end date. Ships remain on station until the president and the defense secretary decide otherwise, according to the Times, a practice the newspaper described as unsustainable.
The Navy operates 11 aircraft carriers in total and has sent four of them to the Middle East during the war. Some of the remaining carriers are undergoing extended shipyard repairs and will not be available to deploy again for years, the Times reported.
One of those four carriers, the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72), spent most of its nine months at sea without a single port call, well beyond the roughly monthly port visits the Navy typically allows crews for rest. The USS George Washington relieved the Lincoln on August 20. The Lincoln docked in Thailand on Wednesday morning, where its crew will get several days of shore leave before the ship continues across the Pacific to its home port in San Diego.

We will add

articles.title: US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
articles.body:
US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
Former White House staffer calls for espionage and cyber options as Washington prepares for a potential Chinese breakthrough
Jacob Stokes, deputy director of the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said at an online event on Thursday that various US agencies, including the Department of Defense and the National Security Agency, should begin assessing what intelligence they need to justify taking such actions.
“Trying to think through the particulars of that will be especially important, in part because it will help policymakers … start to work backwards based on the unique nature of the technology, in the same way that in a past era, policymakers would learn about nuclear weapons and … work backwards from the science to the policy implications,” he said.
In a new CNAS report published last week, the former Obama administration national security staffer called for the US government to consider the feasibility of diplomatic, espionage, cyber and kinetic measures to prevent China from achieving AGI first.

articles.title: General Dynamics gets $194M deal on nuclear missile program
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for fire control engineering support on the SLCM-N nuclear missile program.
- The Navy has set a 2034 target date for delivering the missile, which Congress kept funded after the Biden administration sought to cancel it in 2022.
The U.S. Navy has awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for engineering support work on the Nuclear-Armed, Sea-Launched Cruise Missile program, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee modification adds to a previously awarded unpriced letter contract and covers technical and engineering support for the missile’s Fire Control Subsystem. The $194.1 million figure includes optional line items that may or may not ultimately be exercised. Work will be split between General Dynamics’ facility in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, which will handle 75% of the effort, and a facility in Manassas, Virginia, handling the remaining 25%. The contract is scheduled to run through September 30, 2028.
The Navy is obligating $135.3 million in fiscal 2025 reconciliation research, development, test and evaluation funds at the time of award, none of which will expire at the end of the current fiscal year. The Navy awarded the contract sole source under federal acquisition law, after previously publishing notice of the pending award on the government’s SAM.gov contracting portal. Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office in Washington, D.C., that oversees the service’s ballistic and cruise missile programs, is managing the contract.
The missile at the center of the contract, known as SLCM-N, is a Navy program to develop a low-yield, non-strategic nuclear warhead mounted on a sea-launched cruise missile, intended for deployment on attack submarines and potentially surface ships. The concept was first formally recommended in the Trump administration’s 2018 Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a capability the Navy retired in 2010, when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service.
The Biden administration’s 2022 Nuclear Posture Review recommended canceling SLCM-N, citing cost and questions about the adequacy of the existing nuclear arsenal. Congress rejected that recommendation and continued funding the program through subsequent defense authorization bills, establishing it as a formal program of record in the fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act.
Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of the Navy’s Strategic Systems Programs, testified before Congress in May 2025 that the program had spent the prior year working to define the missile’s overall system architecture, an effort spanning the missile itself, its fire control system, launcher system, platform integration, warhead integration, and associated support equipment and training materials. Wolfe said at the time that the Navy expected to deliver the capability in 2034. Sandia National Laboratories announced in January that the program would use the W80-5 warhead variant.

articles.title: Iran's seven islands strengthen Hormuz control
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The seven islands: what we know about Iran's maritime line controlling Hormuz
As Iran continues to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed, the question is no longer limited to the impact of the closure on global energy markets and the economy.
It has shifted to uncovering the mechanisms Iran uses to control what is currently the world's most sensitive shipping route.
This does not refer to Iran's military capabilities but rather to a complex network of strategic islands whose function Iran has reshaped, turning them into "fixed aircraft carriers" through which it controls shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Geographically, the Strait of Hormuz, located south of Hormozgan province, forms a natural boundary between Iran and Oman.
It is a narrow passage constrained by navigational challenges. Strong water currents and varying depths force giant tankers to follow specific and extremely narrow routes, increasing Tehran's ability to control and monitor them.
The area derives its strategic importance from being the world's second-busiest strait, with about 17 million barrels of crude oil passing through it every day.
This represents 40% of oil transported by sea and about 25% of total global supplies, in a region that alone holds 68% of the world's proven oil and gas reserves.
Characteristics of the Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz is estimated to be 167 kilometres long, while its width varies depending on the area.
It reaches about 95 kilometres at its widest point and narrows to about 33 kilometres at its narrowest.
However, official shipping lanes are much narrower. Each lane designated for vessel traffic is no more than 3 kilometres wide, with a buffer zone separating the inbound and outbound lanes.
The depth of the Strait of Hormuz also varies, reaching more than 60 metres in some areas, while ranging between 30 and 40 metres in shallow areas.
Although this depth is suitable for giant oil tankers and heavy vessels, it forces large ships to follow specific and limited routes, increasing the area's security importance.
The narrowest point of the strait is 21 nautical miles wide, located between Iran's Larak Island and Oman's Greater Quoin Island.
Until 1979, shipping traffic followed the shortest route between the Quoin and Musandam islands.
That year, Oman announced that vessels should pass through an area outside the range of Quoin Island in order to reduce security risks to routes near its islands and territory.
For about 60 years, the shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz passed through Iranian territorial waters.
But Tehran rejected this after it was subjected to war and closed the strait, announcing the opening of a northern route for vessels after they obtained permission from the Iranian navy.
Iran has also held negotiations in recent weeks with Oman to establish a new shipping route.
An agreement was reached, although it was not announced. However, Iranian authorities continue to refuse to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without a response from Washington to its conditions for ending the war permanently, lifting the blockade and sanctions, releasing its frozen assets and other demands.
An island shield to retain Hormuz
Iran's ability to control the Strait of Hormuz is not limited to its coastal capabilities stretching for about 160 kilometres.
A group of Iranian islands also plays a vital role in strengthening this control within these waters.
These islands have given Iran a unique geopolitical position at the entrance to the Gulf, allowing it to control the strait and traffic passing through it.
Seven islands form Iran's curved defensive line in the area for controlling shipping traffic: Hormuz, Larak, Qeshm, Hengam, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa.
The last three islands are disputed between Iran and the United Arab Emirates but are currently under Iranian control.
Four of these islands are located at the entrance to the strait — Hormuz, Qeshm, Larak and Hengam — while the other three disputed islands lie west of this curved line.
The short distances between these islands and the depth of the waters in this area force warships and oil tankers to pass close to them when entering the Strait of Hormuz.
This currently exposes these vessels to threats from fast boats, mines or drones stationed on the islands.
These islands are so important to Iran that former Iranian navigation official Ali Ezzati described them in a statement as "fixed aircraft carriers that cannot be sunk".
The seven islands
1 — Hormuz Island
The island is about 8 kilometres wide and is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas port.
Over the past centuries, Hormuz has been regarded as the key to entering the Gulf. The naming of the strait after it is evidence of this status.
The island is oval-shaped, covering about 42 square kilometres along the strait, and is a tourist destination in southern Iran.
Hormuz City is located in the north and is the island's only population centre. Its population stood at 5,891 according to the 2016 census.
It was under Portuguese occupation for more than a century before Iran regained control of it in 1622 under Shah Abbas.
The Iranian Achaemenid Empire used the island as a naval base more than 2,500 years ago.
Throughout history, it served as a commercial meeting point for traders from India, China and other eastern markets.
The Portuguese viewed it as an impregnable fortress overlooking the meeting point between the Gulf waters and the Indian Ocean.
In the modern era, which has seen the passage of giant oil tankers, Hormuz Island has retained its strategic position despite its relative distance from the deep-water shipping channel.
2 — Larak Island
Larak is located 40 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, the centre of Hormozgan province, 20 kilometres west of Hormuz Island and 12 kilometres east of Qeshm Island.
Larak is unique in being the Iranian island directly adjacent to the deep-water channel in the Strait of Hormuz that is suitable for the passage of giant oil tankers.
Since Iran announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israeli war on 28 February, Larak has been closely linked to developments involving the shipping route.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched an alternative route for shipping through Iranian territorial waters, bypassing the historic route that passed through Omani waters.
The new Iranian route passes south of Larak Island, overlooking the vital energy corridor, making its location the main pillar of Tehran's military system aimed at retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz.
The island lies at the easternmost point of the Gulf and is administratively part of Iran's Hormozgan province.
It is oval-shaped and extends 10.5 kilometres from northeast to southwest.
3 — Qeshm Island
Qeshm is the largest island in the Gulf, with an area twice that of Bahrain, which is the second-largest island in the region.
Qeshm is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, 40 kilometres east of Bandar Lengeh and 31 kilometres east of Greater Tunb.
It is 140 kilometres long.
Qeshm is characterised by its sandy terrain, with hills spread across its central areas.
The highest point is Mount Buko, which rises 405 metres above sea level.
The island covers 1,644 square kilometres and is rich in natural resources, including oil, gas, lead, sulphur and salts.
The island had a population of 148,993 in the 2016 census, with 66,801 living in urban areas and 82,160 in villages and towns.
Over the past decade, Qeshm has become a prominent tourist destination because of its environment and natural and historical sites.
Parts of it have been part of the Global Geoparks Network under the auspices of UNESCO since 2006, as the first geopark in the Middle East.
4 — Hengam Island
Hengam is located just 3 kilometres south of Qeshm Island.
It is about 50 kilometres from Oman's Ghanam Island and shares with Larak Island direct oversight of the deep edge of the shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
The island contains scattered population centres across an area of about 50 square kilometres south of Qeshm.
It contains deposits of salt, soil and lead.
It is 10 kilometres long and between 3 and 6 kilometres wide.
During the Qajar monarchy, Britain established facilities and military bases on the island.
Hengam's coastline is suitable for deploying fleets and naval vessels because of the deep waters surrounding its shores, making it suitable as a berth for warships and submarines.
Its location in the middle of the Gulf waters, adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz and Qeshm, has given it major strategic and military importance.
This has made it historically vulnerable to attempts at control by successive foreign powers.
It was occupied by the Portuguese during the Safavid era and later by the British during the Qajar period.
5 — Greater Tunb
Greater Tunb is one of three islands disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It lies 31 kilometres southwest of Qeshm Island and faces the Strait of Hormuz to the west.
The island is one of the main pillars of Tehran's defence and military doctrine for protecting and managing the strait.
The island is 12 kilometres from Lesser Tunb, 50 kilometres from Abu Musa and about 82 kilometres from Al Hamra Island in Ras Al Khaimah.
It lies north of the Gulf's median line and is roughly circular, covering about 12 square kilometres.
It is predominantly dry and sandy, with little vegetation, while hills in the north reach a maximum height of 53 metres.
6 — Lesser Tunb
Lesser Tunb is the other disputed island between Tehran and Abu Dhabi.
It lies on the northern side of the Gulf's median line, 12 kilometres from Greater Tunb, 50 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 92 kilometres from the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE.
The island covers only about 2 square kilometres, which explains the name "Lesser".
It is roughly triangular in shape, with a width ranging between 1,100 and 1,500 metres.
A dark rocky hill rises 35 metres above sea level in its northwestern part.
Its shores are steep, amid a hot and humid climate, and it has no fresh water.
Unlike Greater Tunb, it is uninhabited and is predominantly used for military and security purposes related to protection and surveillance.
Its spread of rocks and salt domes gives it rugged terrain.
7 — Abu Musa
Abu Musa is the third island disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It forms the westernmost point of Iran's maritime defensive arc and is the final link in the Iranian defence system stationed at the Gulf's gateway.
It is 67 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 62 kilometres from Sharjah port in the UAE.
The island has an airport and a seaport, with regular flights operating between it and Bandar Abbas.
There are also passenger sea transport services using boats and vessels departing from Bandar Lengeh two to three times a week.
Its area is larger than that of both Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb.
It has an irregular shape, while its central and southern areas are flat and sandy.
Its oil resources are limited to the Mubarak field, located offshore to the east of the island.
Its oil is classified as among the highest-quality crude extracted in the Gulf basin.
Revolutionary Guard Navy responsible for security
According to Iran's naval military divisions and formations, the first and fifth naval regions of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy are responsible for securing this curved defensive line and its surrounding area in the Strait of Hormuz.
The First Naval Region, known as "Sahib al-Zaman", is one of the five naval regions of the Revolutionary Guard.
It operates under the supervision of the naval force and the "Khatam al-Anbiya 2" naval headquarters.
The command headquarters of this region is located in Bandar Abbas.
It is the formation closest to the Strait of Hormuz and is responsible for conducting defensive and offensive operations in the area of the passage.
Rear Adm. Abbas Gholamshahi commands it.
On 4 November 2012, the Revolutionary Guard Navy established its Fifth Naval Region, named "Imam Mohammad Baqer", in Bandar Lengeh, overlooking the Gulf waters west of the Strait of Hormuz.
It assigned the region responsibility for controlling the area extending from the end of Qeshm Island, through an area of four islands that became known militarily as the "Naz'at" islands, to the west of Kish Island.
Under this military division, protection and security of the Strait of Hormuz itself was assigned to the First Naval Region as a direct naval mission.
The Fifth Naval Region, meanwhile, was independently tasked with protecting and securing the "Naz'at" island system in the western extension of the Strait of Hormuz.
The four defensive Naz'at islands are Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, Abu Musa and Siri Island.
Tehran relies on a diverse and hybrid arsenal to close or obstruct shipping through this strategic passage.
It combines coastal and mobile weapons along the coast and islands, ranging from underground missile cities and naval and coastal anti-ship missile launchers to fast boats, attack drones and naval mines capable of blocking the route of giant tankers.
Iran also relies on military capabilities beyond its coasts and islands, in both its missile and drone capacities, to tighten its control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akram Nia previously said that "Iran can establish control over the Strait of Hormuz from any point on its territory".
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Rights organizations demand Congress scrap US-Israel military integration bill
articles.body:
Rights organizations demand Congress scrap US-Israel military integration bill
TEHRAN — 56 American civil rights and advocacy organizations have issued a blunt demand to Congress: strip a controversial provision from the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act or risk permanently entrenching Israel inside the Pentagon’s core technology apparatus.
In a joint letter sent to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, the coalition warned that the legislation creates dangerous points of foreign leverage at a moment when American public support for Israel has collapsed following its brutal campaigns of regional aggression.
Designated Section 219 in the House draft and Section 1217 in the Senate version, the proposal establishes the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.
Moving far beyond traditional foreign aid packages subject to yearly congressional debate, the mandate legally enforces co-production plants, joint weapons development, and data fusion across artificial intelligence, cyber warfare, and autonomous systems.
Signatories including Amnesty International USA and the National Lawyers Guild cited Tel Aviv’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank as absolute grounds to reject deeper integration.
A separate policy brief from A New Policy, co-founded by former State Department whistleblower Josh Paul, cautioned that embedding Israeli contractors exposes sensitive American capabilities to counterintelligence risks, disadvantages domestic firms, and systematically hides weapons transfers from public transparency.
While the House of Representatives text of the legislation appoints a Pentagon coordinator, the Senate version goes further by requiring direct, ongoing consultation with Israel’s war minister.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated the clause, boasting it converts his regime from a foreign aid recipient into a full-scale military partner.
A bipartisan amendment introduced by Representatives Thomas Massie (R) and Ro Khanna (D) to remove the provision was buried by House leadership.
With the current ten-year military aid agreement set to expire in 2028, Washington’s pro-Israel establishment is rushing to lock this structural merger into permanent law.
This legislative push comes as public backlash grows over the unprovoked U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and the Resistance Front.
If enacted, Section 219 will bind future administrations to Tel Aviv’s strategic interests regardless of voter demands.

articles.title: Chinese firm claims mass production of new interceptor drone
articles.body:
- Shengying Technology says it has introduced the H-07, an AI-guided interceptor drone the company claims can reach 320 km/h and has entered mass production.
- Interceptor drones have grown rapidly since 2024 as militaries seek cheaper alternatives to missiles for countering mass drone attacks like Russia's Shahed strikes.
Chinese company Shengying Technology says it has introduced a new interceptor drone called the H-07, a high-speed platform designed to shoot down other drones in the final seconds before impact.
Interceptor drones have become one of the fastest-growing categories in air defense over the past two years, driven largely by the need to counter cheap, mass-produced attack drones like Russia’s Iranian-designed Shahed loitering munitions. Traditional air defense missiles, which can cost hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars each, are often too expensive to use against drones that cost a few thousand dollars to build. Interceptor drones aim to close that cost gap by using a cheap aircraft to physically ram or disable another drone in flight.
Ukraine has led much of this development under wartime pressure. Wild Hornets, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, produces roughly 10,000 drones a month, including its Sting interceptor, which the company says has begun shooting down faster, jet-powered variants of the Shahed that were previously considered too fast for propeller-driven interceptors to catch. Ukraine has also fielded the JEDI Shahed Hunter, described as the first pilotless interceptor drone, which receives target data directly from radar stations and can detect and engage threats on its own. Other Ukrainian systems in service include the Baton family of interceptors and the jet-powered Alexa Spatium, launched from a mobile catapult.
The approach has spread beyond Ukraine. Japan’s defense procurement agency selected Terra Drone Corporation’s Terra B1 interceptor for mass production this year after it beat three competing designs in evaluation testing, part of a program aimed specifically at countering long-range, one-way attack drones. In the United States, systems like the foldable SPART interceptor, developed by Ukrainian engineer Yehor Balytskyi’s company Thermopylae Aerospace, have been demonstrated to the U.S. Air Force as a lower-cost alternative to missile-based defenses.
Shengying Technology’s H-07 claims to fit into this same category. According to the company, the drone has entered mass production, though The Defence Blog has not been able to independently confirm this, or the drone’s specifications, deployment, or testing status. No government, military, or third-party source has verified any of the company’s claims.
The H-07 uses a 7-inch airframe. Most first-person-view style interceptor drones use a smaller 5-inch size, and Shengying Technology says the larger frame lets the H-07 reach a top speed of 320 km/h (199 mph), with a cruising speed between 100 and 200 km/h (62 to 124 mph). That would put it in a similar speed range to Ukraine’s SPART interceptor, which the manufacturer has said reaches up to 350 km/h (217 mph).
The company lists a flight range of 15 km (9.3 miles) and a battery life of up to 10 minutes. It puts the drone’s operating altitude between 50 and 2,000 meters (164 to 6,562 feet).
Shengying Technology says the H-07 is built to detect, track, and intercept other drones, including fixed-wing, delta-wing, and multirotor types. The system relies on an onboard AI module based on a YOLO tracking algorithm, a common computer-vision method for real-time object detection. The company says it can lock onto targets from 300 meters (984 feet) away when firing from the ground, and from 200 meters (656 feet) when intercepting another drone in flight.
The drone can launch from the ground or from a launcher, according to the company, and carries a payload of up to 300 grams (0.66 pounds). Its battery is fixed inside the airframe rather than removable, with a direct plug-in charging dock meant to speed up turnaround between flights. Shengying Technology says the H-07 uses three separate cooling methods during high-speed flight: fan cooling for the electronic speed controller, dedicated ventilation openings, and a cooling system for the video transmitter.
The company says the drone’s injection-molded housing and manufacturing tooling are complete and that the platform is ready for large-scale production. It has not disclosed pricing, a customer base, or any confirmed sale, test, or deployment of the H-07 with a military or government buyer.

articles.title: Trump seeks repayment from Europe for past Ukraine aid
articles.body:
- President Trump said the U.S. has "virtually unlimited" munitions and is producing weapons "at levels never seen before" amid Iran war stockpile reports.
- Trump said he will seek repayment from European countries for Ukraine aid, though the U.S. already runs a NATO-backed program where allies pay for U.S. weapons sent to Ukraine.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the United States has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition” and is manufacturing munitions “at levels never seen before,” pushing back against months of reporting that the war with Iran has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles.
Trump made the claims in a Truth Social post published at 7:56 p.m. on September 3, in which he also said the United States would soon resume munitions sales to allies after prioritizing its own stockpiles during the conflict.
“For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place,” Trump wrote. “In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin.”
The post is the latest in a series of denials Trump has issued since March, when reports first surfaced that the intensity of U.S. operations against Iran was drawing down stocks of key munitions. The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post reported in early March that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine had raised concerns about depleted stockpiles ahead of the war’s start. Trump called those reports a “disgrace” at the time and said the U.S. had a “virtually unlimited supply” of certain munitions.
Similar reports resurfaced in July, when The New York Times, NBC News, CBS News and CNN reported that nearly two weeks of daily strikes on Iran had drawn down supplies of defensive interceptors, including Patriot and THAAD missiles, protecting U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz disputed the reporting on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that month, saying anyone leaking such information “deserve[s] to be in jail.”
In August, Reuters reported that the U.S. Army had used “virtually all” of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles during the five-month conflict, citing people familiar with internal military data. Trump responded at the time by calling the U.S. munitions stockpile “massive” and vowing to hunt down “treasonous” leakers.
In Wednesday’s post, Trump also said the Biden administration had given Ukraine and NATO “far more Munitions” at no cost than the U.S. has used in Iran.
“Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for, If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!” Trump wrote.
U.S. military aid to Ukraine under the Biden administration totaled roughly $131 billion, according to figures compiled by the Atlantic Council, most of it disbursed in 2022. European countries have collectively provided more than $227 billion in total aid to Ukraine as of 2025, the same figures show, exceeding the U.S. contribution.
Since July 2025, the United States and NATO have operated the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, a mechanism under which European allies and Canada, not the United States, pay for U.S.-manufactured weapons shipped to Ukraine. The program was established through an agreement between Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. As of October 2025, 26 countries had contributed more than $4 billion through the initiative, according to the Atlantic Council.
