articles.title: The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
articles.body:
The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
Witkoff and Kushner will visit moscow and Kyiv to resume peace talks. The US called on the parties to temporarily halt strikes.
The United States is insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities, and that the Russians halt their missile attacks on Kyiv during the visit of U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to the capitals of the russian federation and Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the NYT.
Details
Two of U.S. President Donald Trump's top emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are heading to moscow and Kyiv this weekend to resume negotiations on a peace deal that would end the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine, officials familiar with the diplomatic efforts said.
Witkoff, the American leader's special envoy, and Kushner, his son-in-law and frequent key negotiator, are expected to meet with Russian President vladimir putin on Saturday. They will then travel to Kyiv for the first time to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
According to officials, talks over the trip have been underway for weeks, with the United States insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities while the two men are in russia, and that the Russians similarly halt their missile attacks on Kyiv. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a trip that has not been officially announced.
The publication notes that it is unclear whether the Americans are offering both presidents new proposals or pushing them to narrow the gap on the remaining issues, including who will ultimately control the Donbas, Ukrainian territory partially occupied by russia.
Although Witkoff and Kushner have traveled to moscow several times, they have not been to Kyiv, despite numerous official invitations. Two weeks ago, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited moscow, where he stayed for only a few hours to meet with his Russian counterpart. Witkoff has seen putin more than half a dozen times.
The meeting is taking place at a dangerous moment in the conflict. For much of the year, Ukraine's attacks on oil refineries and other energy targets have had a devastating impact, forcing Russians to stand in line for hours to get gasoline, if they can find it at all. But the Ukrainians have run out of interceptor missiles to stop Russian missiles raining down on Ukraine, leaving Kyiv and some other cities almost defenseless.
President Trump has sought to bring russia back into the fold: he and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent invited russia to take part in the Group of 20 finance ministers' meeting last week in North Carolina, despite objections from European allies. russia has been excluded from many diplomatic meetings since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
To remind
Zelenskyy stated that U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit moscow on Saturday and that Ukraine guarantees the "normal functioning of Russian airspace," while they are expected in Kyiv on Sunday.
Context
Back in July, it was reported that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner agreed to visit Kyiv for the first time as part of peace efforts to end the war.
At the end of August, it was reported that Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Ukraine, amid intensified russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv, had been postponed but not canceled.
On September 3, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that a visit by U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv could take place in the coming days, but that they would first visit moscow.
On September 3, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced "new momentum" in peace efforts to end russia's war against Ukraine, with the return of an active political and diplomatic phase, but noted that achieving this without the participation of the American side was unrealistic.
On September 4, a source in the Russian media reported that American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit Russia and Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, September 5 and 6.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis launch first major offensive in four years
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis launch first major offensive in four years
Yemen's Houthis have launched their first large-scale offensive since 2022 following a breakdown in a ceasefire with the government earlier in July.
The offensive, launched on Thursday, saw Houthi forces fire heavy artillery, ballistic missiles, and carry out drone strikes in an attempt to gain ground along the Red Sea in Taiz province.
Around 129 people have been killed, according to an AFP tally, including 66 government soldiers, 62 Houthi militants, and one civilian, though Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported that dozens of civilians had been killed and wounded in a Houthi ballistic missile strike on a restaurant in the city of Mokha.
The city of Mokha is reported to be a key objective for the Houthi offensive, a key port controlled by the government on the Red Sea, with the Houthis assaulting positions on the Taiz-Mokha road to reach the city.
Fighting has also been raging in the hills around the city of Taiz, with government forces launching counterattacks to retake several key areas in the neighbouring Jabal Habashi district that had fallen after Houthi assaults.
Government attacks were also launched in the al-Ma'afer district and the Maqbanah district.
In response to the Houthi offensive, the government has sent reinforcements to the region, including the pro-Government National Shield Forces and Giant's Brigades.
Mohammad al-Basha of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report told AFP that the Houthis wanted to extend their control over the Bab al-Mandab.
"The Houthis feel that if they capture Bab al-Mandab or Mokha port, they will be in a better position to negotiate with the government and the Saudis."
This was echoed by Ibrahim Jalal, Lead Researcher at the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends, who said on X that "a sustained advance here would fracture the [government's] Taiz-Coast defensive network, isolate Al-Mokha and Al-Khokha from reinforcement and resupply, and create a landward approach form which the Houthis could place the southern Res Sea coast and ultimately the Bab al-Mandab axis under greater military pressure, including red sea shipping".
"Clearly, the immediate Yemeni Armed Forces priority is to restore the pre-attack line, secure the Taiz–coast corridor and deny the Houthis any durable foothold from which to sustain pressure toward Al-Mokha and the southern Red Sea," he added.
Yemen's civil war unravelled earlier in July after Saudi airstrikes targeted Sanaa airport in a bid to stop a flight from Iran carrying Houthi delegates and suspected Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps members from landing in the Houthi-controlled territory.
The Houthis responded by announcing a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have attacked shipping in the Red Sea.
Yemen has been in a state of civil war since 2014, when a Houthi offensive ousted the Yemeni government from the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led intervention in 2015.
The country remains one of the worst humanitarian crisis points in the world, relying heavily on outside humanitarian aid.

articles.title: Germany launches mass production of strike drones for Ukraine
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Germany has begun mass production of more than 5,000 medium- and long-range strike drones for Ukraine, defense company Auterion and its Ukrainian joint-venture partner Airlogix said.
The first units have already been manufactured in the greater Munich area under a German government order that industry sources estimate at about €300 million ($348 million).
The companies said the contract is due to be completed by mid-2027.
The drones are part of Germany’s military assistance to Ukraine, amid the conflict with Russia that began in February 2022.
The joint venture, founded in February, said it expects follow-on orders and a long-term commissioning.
“Germany now has a production line for affordable precision weapons in large quantities,” Auterion Chief Executive Lorenz Meier told local media.
“We will deliver already proven and tested systems this year -- at costs and at a manufacturing pace that actually make large stockpiles for deterrence possible,” Meier added.
Production is underway at an undisclosed site near Munich and is also planned at a second plant in eastern Germany, German news agency dpa reported.
Two models are being manufactured, according to company sources.
One has a medium range, while the other can fly up to 1,500 kilometers (about 930 miles), the sources said.
Auterion supplies the software and operating system, while Airlogix provides the hardware.
The one-way strike drones carry explosives and are designed to hit and destroy their targets rather than return.
Artificial intelligence is intended to keep the drones on course even when electronic warfare systems attempt to jam them.

articles.title: Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
articles.body:
Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
BEIRUT/JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Israel's military has cleared Hezbollah fighters holed up in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Friday, though the Iran-backed group did not immediately comment.
Israel had said Hezbollah fighters were embedded in tunnels under the ridge, which overlooks a wide area and had become one of the most hotly contested areas in the Israel-Hezbollah war, despite a ceasefire announced in June.
Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli assault on its Hezbollah allies' positions within the ridge.
"The mission was completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists," Katz said on social media, after a statement by the military late on Thursday saying it had operational control of the ridge.
The military said some Hezbollah fighters had been "eliminated", while others had fled.
A Lebanese military officer said Israeli troops had seized the southern entrances to the complex and could monitor the northern entrances through surveillance drones.
The complex included various tunnels and storage areas, some of which were not connected to one another, and it was unclear how far the troops had penetrated, and whether any fighters were still there, or might have booby-trapped parts of the complex, the officer said.
Hezbollah did not immediately respond to a request for comment and Reuters was not able to verify the status of the ridge independently.
The Shi'ite Muslim group is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores within the ridge and had said it would resist any Israeli assault.
ISRAEL RELEASES FIVE LEBANESE DETAINEES
Israel has expanded its military presence across swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against Hezbollah in March.
On Friday, Israeli authorities released four people who had been held in Israeli prisons after being detained by Israeli troops in southern Lebanon. They were transferred to Lebanese authorities via the International Committee of the Red Cross, a day after one Lebanese man was released.
Israel said on Thursday that none of the five had been found to have ties to militant groups.
Hussein Ayyash, a 33-year-old released on Friday, said he was driving in the southern Lebanese town of Kfar Tebnit nearly three months ago when Israeli soldiers approached and ordered him out of his car.
He said he was blindfolded and handcuffed, and then slept several days in various homes in southern Lebanon before being transferred into Israel and held in solitary confinement, sometimes for up to 30 days.
"Then they move you to prison, a normal room. There are places, called a cage, you sit in it. There are some people -- Syrian nationals, Lebanese nationals, Palestinian nationals -- all the nationalities, the different ones, are in prison. You get moved from room to room every once in a while, every 40 days, 30 days," Ayyash told Reuters.
He said he was asked whether he had ties to Hezbollah, and was not tortured but suffered mental strain.
"You have to talk. They have all the information. Psychological pressure isn't easy -- you're in a country that isn't yours, you're with people you don't know, and you don't know when you'll leave," he said.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters questions about Ayyash's detention.
Ayyash's mother, Layla Hamdan, 58, said she was delighted her son was back, adding: "God willing, may all the hostages returned to their mothers and their families."
ISRAEL SEEKS REMAINS OF JEWISH LEADERS
The release of the detainees is part of confidence-building measures agreed in U.S.-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel.
A Lebanese committee advocating for Lebanese in Israeli custody says Israel has detained dozens of people inside Lebanon over the last six months. Some have been released after days or weeks, others remain in Israeli custody.
The ICRC said on Friday it had not had access to anyone in Israeli detention since October 2023.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said those freed this week were among a "first batch", suggesting more could be coming.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Lebanon would also transfer the remains of Jewish figures killed in Lebanon in the 1980s to Israel, although there were no details of names or any timeframe. REUTERS

articles.title: Vance says US not at 'war', scores killed in Houthi offensive
articles.body:
US Vice President JD Vance on Thursday declined to provide a timeline for when the conflict with Iran would be over, pushing back against calling the hostilities a "war".
Speaking at the White House, Vance said the US had ended major combat operations against Iran, though said Washington was focussed on preventing Iran from disrupting global trade.
"I wouldn't call it a war," Vance said. "Right now there's no active shooting. I recognize there's been places where this has flared up."
Asked repeatedly about the timeline on the war, Vance said an end would require a halt in Iranians shooting at commercial shipping.
"When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don't know the answer to that question," he said.
He also ruled out any negotiations as long as Tehran continued to target commercial shipping.
Elsewhere, a renewed assault by Yemen's Houthi rebels has seen at least 81 people killed in clashes with Saudi-backed government forces, military and medical sources said on Friday.
The rebels are now trying to cement their hold over one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, which they have disrupted with attacks on passing vessels since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.
Yemen ministry condemns Houthi attacks on civilians
Yemen's Ministry of Human Rights on Friday condemned a military escalation by the Houthi group in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen, accusing the group of targeting residential areas, displacement camps and an educational facility, as well as killing a civilian sniper fire.
In a statement carried by the state-run Saba News Agency, the ministry said the escalation involved artillery and missile attacks and drone strikes targeting areas in the districts of Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, Al-Kadha and Al-Dhubab.
It said the attacks violated international humanitarian law and international human rights law.
Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said on Friday that Tehran exercises full sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, stressing that Iran is "standing firm" against US "arrogance".
He added that management of the strategic waterway would "continue with full strength until all foreign forces leave the region".
As Israeli authorities and settlers move to annex more Palestinian land, a non-profit group is threatening to sue the UK government's tax agency for allegedly allowing products from illegal Israeli settlements to enter the United Kingdom tariff-free.
The Global Echo Litigation Centre, a non-profit legal group dedicated to using litigation to take on Israeli occupation, wrote to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) saying that agricultural goods from these illegal settlements in areas like the occupied West Bank entered the UK while violating trade rules.
A four-year investigation by the non-profit found that some products that were labelled “Israeli” actually came from the occupied Palestinian territories. After the findings, the group slammed HMRC's process for verifying the origin of Israeli products as “flawed".
In correspondence seen exclusively by, a letter from law firm Leigh Day, representing the non-profit, said the flawed process meant settlement products “unlawfully benefitted” from tax treatment.
"Our client believes HMRC’s approach to compliance and enforcement regarding such imports to the UK risks leaving the preferential tariff system open to misuse," Tom Short, solicitor at Leigh Day, told The New Arab.
More than 120 people have been killed since Yemen's Houthis launched an advance a day ago on the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, in the deadliest clashes for years between the rebels and government forces.
The toll rose to 129 on Friday, according to AFP news agency, up from an earlier count of 81.
A Yemeni military official speaking on condition of anonymity told AFP that 66 of his men had been killed, while medical and military sources close to the Houthis said at least 62 militants had died. Another medical source said a civilian had also been killed.
UAE pardons Egyptian-Turkish poet facing 10 years in jail
Egyptian-Turkish poet Abdulrahman Youssef al-Qaradawi was pardoned by United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on Friday, state news agency WAM said, a week after receiving a 10-year jail sentence following his extradition from Lebanon.
Qaradawi, the son of late senior Muslim cleric Youssef al-Qaradawi, was arrested in Lebanon in December 2024 after making critical comments about the UAE, Saudi Arabian and Egyptian authorities in a video posted online.
He was extradited in January 2025, facing charges of "engaging in activities that aim to stir and undermine public security", WAM said at the time.
Rights groups and UN experts had called for Qaradawi's release, saying he had been arrested after exercising his right to free expression.
His father, who died in 2022, was a spiritual guide to the Muslim Brotherhood, championed the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, and drew the ire of rulers in Egypt and the Gulf with his Islamist preaching.
Abdulrahman Youssef al-Qaradawi [Getty]
US Treasury sanctions Turkish bank over alleged Iran links
The US Treasury on Friday announced new sanctions targeting a Turkish bank over its alleged ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), part of Washington's renewed attempts to economically isolate Tehran.
"Financial institutions continue to find out the hard way that we are serious about Operation Economic Outcast," said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime."
Israel releases four Lebanese civilians, other MENA updates
Israel has released four Lebanese civilians detained by its forces in southern Lebanon, handing them over to Lebanese authorities on Friday.
The release follows US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon, with another round of negotiations expected in Rome later this month.
Meanwhile, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains low following renewed US-Iran attacks, while US diesel prices reached a record average of $5.85 a gallon.
Fighting has also intensified in Yemen between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and government forces near Taiz. Both sides have suffered casualties, officials said.
The price of diesel -- the vital fuel used for road hauling, agriculture and construction -- hit a new record Friday in the United States.
The cost is now $5.85 a gallon, up from $3.71 a year ago, the AAA motorists' association said.
Prices at the pump have jumped since US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran from late February sparked Tehran's retaliation in blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for energy transit.
Global oil prices have remained high, and surged this week on a fresh escalation in fighting.
US Vice President JD Vance blamed Iran when asked about earlier comments by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Americans could potentially see $3 gas again by Labor Day, which falls on September 7.
Katz hails capture of Lebanese highland for 'security zone'
Israel's defence minister on Friday hailed the capture of a strategic highland in Lebanon as solidifying Israel's "security zone" in Lebanon and vowed that troops would not leave it.
"The capture of the Ali Tahar ridge marks the completion of the phase of securing control in the security zone in southern Lebanon," Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement.
Four Lebanese citizens held by Israel were released and handed over to the International Committee of the Red Cross Friday as part of a deal between the two countries. In return, Lebanon agreed to search for the bodies of Jewish Lebanese citizens who went missing during the country's civil war decades ago.
Dozens of Lebanese prisoners are believed to be held in Israeli detention centers, including civilians. A total of five detainees are being released under the current deal, all civilians.
Israeli police killed a Palestinian man in central Jerusalem, accusing the man of attempting to carry out a knife attack.
The incident took place overnight near Damascus Gate, which leads into Jerusalem's Old City, Israeli police said, adding that the dead man was a 33-year-old from Jerusalem.
The Palestinian news agency Wafa also reported the death, saying police had set up a military cordon around Damascus Gate and the Old City.

articles.title: Ukraine adopts two-tier air raid alert system as Russia’s mass drone attacks become the new normal
articles.body:
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted a decision to introduce two levels of air alerts, with yellow for drone attacks and red for a heightened threat of missile or combined strikes, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on 3 September. Under the yellow level, designated businesses can operate if they meet safety requirements, while a red alert will require work to stop and people to move to shelters.
Russia continues to attack Ukrainian cities with drones and other long-range weapons, repeatedly disrupting civilian and economic activity. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia is using mass drone attacks to wear down civilian life and economic activity, while the existing system of signaling all aerial threats in the same way no longer fits Russia's tactics.
How it will work
Businesses cleared to operate under a yellow alert must ensure staff and visitors can reach shelters. Where that access is missing, the Cabinet is giving businesses three months to provide it.
The General Staff, the Air Force, the government, the Defense Ministry, the Interior Ministry, and the State Emergency Service will set the specific indicators for declaring each level weekly, Zelenskyy said.
What still has to be worked out
Zelenskyy also directed officials to develop geographic targeting for alerts, so warnings can be limited to areas facing an actual threat. The measure is still being worked out and is not yet part of the new system.
The new approach is intended to allow economic activity to continue during drone threats while preserving stricter measures for more serious attacks. The government has not yet finalized which businesses will qualify to remain open under a yellow alert or all of the criteria for applying the two levels.

articles.title: British aircraft carrier deploying to deter Russia
articles.body:
HMS Queen Elizabeth will sail from Portsmouth this weekend for a three-month deployment around the UK and northern Europe, with the Royal Navy saying the carrier will strengthen NATO deterrence, readiness and collective defence.
The 65,000-tonne aircraft carrier is due to begin leaving Portsmouth Naval Base at 6.20pm on Saturday 5 September with more than 800 sailors aboard. The deployment will combine advanced warfighting training with the ship’s new role as NATO’s afloat command platform for the Allied Response Force.
Over the next three months, Queen Elizabeth will operate around British and northern European waters alongside allied forces, developing the crew’s ability to conduct high-end naval operations and command a multinational force in a crisis. The Royal Navy stated that the deployment would see the carrier “conduct an intensive programme of training and operations, working alongside Allies to enhance collective security, deterrence and readiness.”
Queen Elizabeth assumed the NATO command ship role for the Allied Response Force in July, the first time either of the Queen Elizabeth-class carriers has performed the task. During the deployment, the ship will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together if NATO was required to respond to a crisis.
Captain Claire Thompson, Commanding Officer of HMS Queen Elizabeth, said:
“We’ve returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training. Sailing this autumn is a key milestone for both our NATO commitment, as the Afloat Command Platform and also on our journey back to the Royal Navy’s ‘very high readiness’ aircraft carrier, a duty we will resume from our sister ship HMS Prince of Wales in 2027. Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of NATO should it be required.”
The carrier will also undertake advanced training under the Royal Navy’s Fleet Operational Standards and Training organisation, covering the full range of modern naval warfare. The programme is intended to prepare Queen Elizabeth for higher readiness and eventual return to the UK’s principal carrier role. Training will continue into 2027, including participation in major NATO exercises, before Queen Elizabeth takes over from HMS Prince of Wales as the UK’s flagship and high-readiness strike carrier later that year.
The Royal Navy said British forces are already contributing to NATO deterrence across Europe, with more than 1,000 UK personnel serving in NATO command posts and Britain leading the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps from Gloucestershire.
UK forces also include an 800-strong battlegroup in Estonia, RAF Typhoon fighters deployed to defend NATO airspace over Romania, and P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft operating around the Baltic.
The UK also assigns its nuclear deterrent to the defence of the Alliance and, under plans confirmed in the Defence Investment Plan, intends to join NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft nuclear mission with F-35A fighters.
Queen Elizabeth’s autumn deployment will therefore combine NATO command duties with the process of returning the carrier and her crew to very high readiness, while maintaining a British carrier presence in northern European waters as NATO continues to strengthen deterrence and its ability to respond rapidly to a crisis.

articles.title: Witkoff and Kushner set to visit Moscow then Kyiv on Sunday
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
“We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote.
No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict.
Advertisement
Russian state news agency TASS reported that Witkoff and Kushner “intend to travel to Moscow and Kyiv on September 5-6.”
The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks. Witkoff made several trips to Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025 and early 2026 and met with Zelenskyy in the U.S., Germany and France. This will be their first trip to Kyiv.
After Trump returned to office in early 2025, the U.S. launched an intensive push for a Russia-Ukraine peace deal focused on territorial compromises, security guarantees for Ukraine and postwar reconstruction. Washington initially put heavy pressure on Kyiv to accept the proposals, but by early 2026, the talks broke down.
In recent weeks, Washington has renewed its efforts to engage with Moscow, with CIA Director John Ratcliffe visiting the Russian capital in late August. Ratcliffe used the trip to press Russia to reduce its military and economic support to Iran and urge it not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies.

articles.title: Cabinet proposes NT$145.7 billion in additional Taiwan defense spending
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet on Thursday approved NT$145.7 billion (US$4.64 billion) in additional defense spending for 2026, including funding for missile systems and uncrewed vehicles excluded from a special defense procurement law.
The Cabinet approved a record NT$607.6 billion in supplemental spending for the 2026 central government budget, per Rti. The defense allocation includes NT$4.1 billion for personnel, NT$8.2 billion for operations, and NT$133.4 billion for military investment.
The personnel funding includes NT$2.5 billion to expand military recruitment and NT$1.6 billion to increase allowances for combat units and eligible personnel. The operating budget includes NT$7.3 billion for ammunition and NT$900 million for the Taiwan Tactical Network integration project.
The military investment portion includes NT$13 billion for seven projects, NT$55.9 billion for three types of drones, and NT$64.5 billion for two classified projects, Rti reported. The package also includes funding for the Integrated Battle Command System, Chien Kung missiles, and uncrewed vehicles covered by the recently passed unmanned vehicle law.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) directed that the systems be included because national defense could not wait for the legislative process, according to Rti. The Legislative Yuan previously approved a scaled-back version of the special defense procurement law that excluded the unmanned systems and other domestically developed weapons.
Lee said the government would review the legislation and its implementation after receiving it Wednesday. She said the supplemental budget was intended to make up for delays in military buildup.
Department of Strategic Planning Director Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啓) said the special defense budget was originally NT$1.25 trillion and covered 23 items, per CNA. Because the full amount was not approved, the 13 items for domestic production, commercial purchases, and Taiwan-US joint development were included in the supplemental budget.
Huang said the supplemental budget was proposed primarily based on the military buildup schedule, as uncrewed vehicle units began forming last year and all units were in place as of January. The military plans to procure 40,000 coastal attack drones, 600 coastal reconnaissance drones, and 100 small one-way unmanned surface vessels in 2027, per Storm Media.

articles.title: Chinese radios power Russia’s longer-range drone strikes
articles.body:
- Russia has extended live drone operator control to 150-175 kilometers using Chinese-made mesh radios, roughly double its 2025 range, according to KI Insights.
- The mesh network technology has let Russia redirect Geran-2 and Gerber drones toward mid-range strikes that have disabled over 250 Ukrainian gas stations.
Russian forces have significantly extended how far they can fly and control attack drones inside Ukraine over the past year by switching many of them to mesh-network radios, according to a report from Kyiv-based analytics firm KI Insights.
The technology, called MIMO mesh radio, lets a drone act as a mobile relay point in a decentralized radio network rather than depending on a single, direct radio link back to its operator. Since 2025, Russia has fitted the system to several of its drone types, including the Geran and Gerbera strike drones, the Orlan and Supercam reconnaissance drones, and the Lancet, Scalpel and Molniya models, according to the report, authored by Etienne Hertz, a radio-frequency specialist based in Ukraine.
Ukrainian military sources told KI Insights that a chain of mesh-linked drones can now maintain live operator control up to 150 to 175 kilometers (93 to 109 miles) from the farthest Russian ground station, roughly double what Russian mesh networks could manage in 2025. Russian pilots have demonstrated real-time control over Geran and Gerbera drones flying near the city of Dnipro, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the front line, the report said.
On July 17, a Geran drone operated by Russia’s 50th Separate Operational Brigade of Unmanned Systems Forces, known as Varyag, struck a gas condensate plant near Seleshchyna in Ukraine’s Poltava region while flying 125 kilometers (78 miles) from Russian-held territory and maintaining direct operator control the entire time, according to the report. KI Insights said Varyag has increasingly struck targets in Ukraine’s Sumy and Chernihiv regions rather than its earlier focus further south, a shift the firm said could signal Russian preparation to intensify operations along a northern front.
The mesh radios enabling this reach are not Russian-made. KI Insights traced the hardware to two Chinese manufacturers, Shenzhen Sinosun Technology and Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, with a Saint Petersburg-based company called Ajax Technologies distributing some of the radios inside Russia. The report said Russia remains fully dependent on Chinese components for the underlying mesh radio hardware, even if Russian engineers have contributed to how the systems are integrated into drones.
Mesh radios cost considerably more than the alternative many drone operators use, SpaceX’s Starlink satellite terminals, which run slightly above $400. Russia’s Chinese-made mesh modems cost between $2,000 and $12,000, and their range drops off sharply beyond 100 to 200 kilometers, unlike Starlink’s near-global coverage. Mesh links also carry higher latency, or delay, than Starlink, making them less useful against fast-moving targets, according to the report. Bureau 1440, a Russian satellite company, is expected to extend Russian drone operator range further later this year through a new satellite constellation called Rassvet, KI Insights said.
The report highlighted one specific case: Russian forces in the Zaporizhzhia area have converted the low-cost Molniya 2R drone, which normally costs $800 to $1,200, into an airborne mesh relay node by adding cameras, onboard computer-vision processors and a mesh radio, raising its cost to an estimated $4,000 to $5,000. Because the modified Molniya can both process its own sensor data and forward signals from other drones dozens of kilometers away, it lets Russian forces maintain aerial relay coverage cheaply and repeatedly, without relying on more expensive, harder-to-replace drones like the Orlan.
KI Insights said the range and video quality this technology provides has helped Russia shift many of its piston-engine Geran-2 and Gerber drones away from long-range strikes deep into Ukraine, where Ukrainian air defenses intercept 90 to 95% of incoming drones, and toward mid-range attacks on stationary infrastructure such as passenger trains and gas stations. The firm said this campaign has disabled or damaged more than 250 gas stations across northeastern, eastern, central and southern Ukraine.
KI Insights assessed that Russia’s mesh-drone capability is moving toward technological parity with NATO drone fleets and could pose risks to NATO logistics in a future conflict involving Russia or Belarus, though the firm noted Russian video links still carry higher latency than NATO systems typically tolerate. The report did not specify a timeline for when Russian capabilities might reach that level, or how Ukraine’s own electronic warfare units plan to counter the expanding mesh networks.

articles.title: Beyond missiles: Why Israel’s civilian infrastructure needs stronger defenses - editorial
articles.body:
When five major Mediterranean desalination plants went offline earlier this week, household taps didn't run dry. It exposed why water, electricity, food, and shelters must be treated as matters of national security. That is precisely why the incident should be treated as a warning rather than dismissed as a crisis successfully contained.
The plants were forced offline after unusually high seawater turbidity, apparently caused by microalgae carried north from the Nile Delta. Some subsequently resumed operating, but three remained offline on Wednesday.
The authorities protected residential supply, while municipalities were instructed to reduce nonessential consumption, and agricultural water was temporarily cut in parts of the country. Negev farmers warned that crops at the height of the growing season could suffer irreversible damage within a day.
On one level, the outcome demonstrates the water system’s strength: Israel maintained household supplies even after losing most of its desalination capacity. That is a considerable accomplishment in a dry country that once lived at the mercy of rainfall.
Exposing the concentration beneath the success
But the incident also exposed the concentration beneath that success. A small number of large facilities produce much of Israel's drinking water, and all require usable seawater, electricity, and functioning pumping infrastructure. A single natural event was enough to interrupt several at once.
A recent preprint by researchers from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Max Planck Institutes modeled scenarios in which drought, electricity disruptions, war, cyberattacks, and marine pollution overlap. The research has not yet undergone peer review, but the question it raises is immediately relevant: Is Israel preparing for several systems to fail at once, or is each ministry still preparing for its own isolated scenario?
Israel understandably speaks about national security through the language of armies, borders, intelligence, and missile defense; those threats are real and immediate. But civilians cannot live beneath Iron Dome alone.
Security also means that the lights remain on, hospitals keep functioning, food reaches supermarkets, and families have somewhere protected to go when the air-raid siren sounds. These are not softer alternatives to national defense; rather, they are what allow a country to absorb an attack and continue operating.
Recent State Comptroller’s Reports have revealed a recurring weakness in precisely these areas. In January, the comptroller found that one-third of Israelis lacked adequate access to standard protected spaces, and that 12% of public shelters were unfit for use. A February audit found that emergency planning for the electricity sector had not kept pace with changes in the industry, and that responsibility for critical diesel stocks remained unresolved years after the government ordered it transferred.
No single government body overseeing the full picture of emergency food security
Last October a report found no single government body was overseeing the full picture of emergency food security, and there was no long-term national strategy. A separate February audit found that prior to the October 7 massacre, Israel did not have an approved operational plan for mass civilian evacuation, leaving local authorities to improvise as some 210,000 residents were displaced.
Since then, some of the relevant government bodies have taken steps. The Energy and Infrastructure Ministry, for example, has cited a NIS 1 billion program launched during the war to strengthen infrastructure and emergency stocks. This week’s uninterrupted household water supply also reflects serious advance planning.
The argument, therefore, is not that nothing works; it is that Israel repeatedly relies on capable workers and emergency improvisation to close gaps that should have been resolved beforehand. Across sectors, responsibility remains divided, plans age without being updated, and corrective action accelerates only once the danger becomes visible.
That is partly a problem of political incentives. Air-defense procurements and military operations produce announcements that maintenance, redundancy, and coordination between ministries rarely do. When they succeed, nothing dramatic happens: The tap runs, the refrigerator stays cold, and the local authority knows what to do.
With a little under two months until the October 27 election, parties asking Israelis to trust them with national security should be expected to address this side of it as well. They should explain who will hold binding responsibility for civilian preparedness, which deficiencies have been corrected, what deadlines remain, and how weaker municipalities will be brought up to standard.
The desalination disruption should not be forgotten when the last plant returns to operation. Israel’s strength is measured not only by whether it can strike its enemies or intercept their weapons, but by whether ordinary life can continue under pressure.

articles.title: Pacific leaders voice concern over Chinese missile test but stop short of condemnation
articles.body:
In brief
- The Pacific Islands Forum has agreed to "register concern" over a Chinese missile test in July.
- The statement falls short of condemnation, and Nauru dissented the clause.
The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) has wrapped up with most nations agreeing to "register concern" on China's recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test, "which overflew a number of members without adequate notice".
"Leaders call on all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance, including through the provision of advance notification of a test at least 24 hours in accordance with international practice," the communique says, as read out by Palau's President and PIF chair Surangel Whipps Junior, after the closing ceremony.
But it was not unanimous.
In a rare move for the usually consensus-based forum, Nauru was the only one of 18 PIF members to dissent from the clause.
Kiribati and Nauru were the only two Pacific nations that had previously blocked a draft PIF statement in the immediate aftermath of Beijing's test, a move that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had been advocating for.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
However the statement went further than analysts and government sources had expected; the PIF foreign ministers' meeting statement in August was broader, discussing ballistic missile testing in the region, but had stopped short of singling out a particular ICBM or referencing a notice period for nations to undergo any testing.
Whipps also hit back against China's comments that Palau sensationalised its ballistic missile test, saying: "There's no sensationalism, it's just stating the facts."
"The Pacific Islands weren't informed [of the test]. The ones that were informed were informed late, and so I think the message from the forum is clear: that transparency needs to happen."
Intelligence shows the nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile test in July flew over the Philippines, Palau and Micronesia's airspace before landing in the Pacific Ocean.
Several nations had criticised the test, just the second since 1980.
The response has become something of a litmus test for PIF and its members for their strategic positioning.
The communique's relevant clause includes a reference to the Fiji-led Ocean of Peace declaration made last year, which states the region should be free from coercion and militarisation.
However, it doesn't name China, nor does it use heftier diplomatic language than "concern".
While Australian officials were happy with the agreed statement, it fell short of some pre-retreat expectations, including those of the host, Palau.
Whipps made his displeasure with the test clear, which followed a 2024 effort.
"They sent a missile next to French Polynesia, another one next to Tuvalu, crossing over our airspace. They never bothered to tell us that's what's happening," he said.
"I said 'there's a lot of space between Japan and Guam, why don't you send it there? Why does it have to come to the middle of the Pacific when last year we just signed a declaration of peace?'
"We don't want our backyard, our homes, to be threatened and really disrespected."
Whipps said "a unified Pacific voice" would be critical to get Beijing to "respect sovereignty".
No region-wide pact
In other decisions of the leaders' retreat, PIF will categorise external powers, currently known as "dialogue partners", as either strategic or sector partners.
The 13 strategic partners will be China, the US, France, Germany, the UK, the EU, Canada, Japan, India, Indonesia, Singapore, South Korea and the UAE.
Those partners will be able to continue to travel to leaders' meetings, while sector partners will be referred to the annual foreign ministers gathering.
A region-wide security pact, championed by Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, did not progress — as expected, given Wale's absence.
A proposal to bring the Australia-backed Joint Heads of Pacific Security under the Pacific Islands Forum has also garnered some support.

articles.title: Schiess Sworn in as New Space Force Chief: ‘We Must Grow with Intention’
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md.—Gen. Douglas A. Schiess assumed leadership of the Space Force on Sept. 3, succeeding Gen. B. Chance Saltzman as Chief of Space Operations during a change of responsibility ceremony here.
Schiess is just the third CSO in the Space Force’s history since the service was created in 2019. In his first address to Guardians, he emphasized the important role space has come to play in modern military operations—and the growing threats it attracts from adversaries intent on targeting space assets in orbit and on the ground.
“Every day, our potential adversaries advance their efforts to disrupt, degrade, and destroy our space capabilities, and they try to add to their own capacity to exploit space to their advantage,” Schiess said. “We cannot, we will not let that happen.”
A career space operator, Schiess has performed a number of missions in his career including missile warning, GPS, command and control, and launch. In 2023, he became the first commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, USSF’s component to the U.S. Space Command combatant command. Most recently, he served as deputy CSO for operations, developing and implementing the policies that guide Space Force operations around the world.
That experience, he said, will inform the way he leads Guardians trained “to operate in the cold, dark vacuum of space” from operations centers on the ground that are also under threat—as evidenced in ongoing operations in the Middle East, where Iran has targeted ground-based space and missile defense infrastructure.
“Our Guardians operate from the ground, some in harm’s way—some in harm’s way today—and they require battlefield skills and the warrior mentality as much as our Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and Coast Guardsmen in our sister services,” he said.
Schiess’ emphasis on the growing threats and the warfighting contributions of Guardians continue themes that his predecessor, Saltzman, repeated often throughout his tenure.
Over the past four years, Saltzman helped grow the Space Force from 8,000 uniformed Guardians to 10,000—and he has positioned the force for even more expansion in the coming years. The service is on a path to double in size to 20,000 Guardians over the next five years, and its $71 billion budget request for fiscal 2027 is more than twice what USSF requested last year, as demand increases for space capabilities.
Speaking during the ceremony, Saltzman said he’s proud of the progress the Space Force has made, evidenced in recent months by its delivery of “critical effects” during multiple operations.
“We delivered critical effects on time and on target under fire, and we sustained that effort,” Saltzman said. “When called to action, the U.S. Space Force was ready, combat capable, and mission effective, and that about says it all.”
Saltzman praised Schiess’ leadership, operational experience, and genuine concern for Guardians, their families, and the joint and allied partners they serve alongside.
“He knows how to build teams, how to drive performance, and how to coax bureaucracies into mission success,” Saltzman said. “He has the expertise to make wise decisions. . . . He cares deeply for the people that do the work.”
In his first message to the force, issued shortly after his swearing in, Schiess harkened back to the Space Force’s early days and looked ahead to the future, calling on Guardians to “capitalize on our foundation and evolve to meet the demands of a new era.”
“As we drive our deliberate growth and execution, we will arm our Guardians to acquire, field, operate, and exploit the full spectrum of capabilities required to secure decisive space superiority,” he said. “Integrating into the Joint Force demands a rapid scaling of both our manpower and space capabilities. We must grow with intention, leveraging our industry partnerships to advance our weapon systems and the way we fight.”
Along with Schiess’ ascension to the service chief job this week, the Department of the Air Force also welcomed its assistant secretary for space acquisition and integration, Erich Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn in at the Pentagon on Aug. 31. Hernandez-Baquero, who will oversee a growing space acquisition portfolio, fills a position that has been vacant since January 2025, though several officials have served in an acting capacity.

articles.title: Ukraine is "optimistic" about new U.S. sanctions against Russia, but obstacles remain
articles.body:
Ukraine is "optimistic" about new U.S. sanctions against Russia, but obstacles remain
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Senate approved a bill on sanctions against Russia and Iran, but its consideration in the House of Representatives remains uncertain. Vlasiuk said there is broad bipartisan support for increasing pressure on Moscow.
Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk is optimistic about the prospects for the sweeping sanctions bill against Russia in the U.S. Congress, despite growing uncertainty over when the House of Representatives will consider it. UNN reports this, citing RFE/RL.
How the sanctions are progressing
Ukraine's top sanctions official spent this week in Washington, meeting with lawmakers and congressional staff amid hopes of advancing Lindsey Graham's 2026 Sanctions Against Russia and Iran Act.
The legislation was passed by the Senate on August 7 by an overwhelming majority (86-11), reflecting rare bipartisan agreement. The bill would give the U.S. president additional powers to impose "punitive" tariffs on countries that continue to buy Russian fossil fuels. It also contains provisions targeting Iran, which, according to Vlasiuk, cooperates closely with Moscow in the military-industrial sphere.
But the measure will face a more difficult path in the House of Representatives, where some Democrats have raised concerns about provisions that would give U.S. President Donald Trump additional authority to impose tariffs.
In addition, on September 3, Republican leaders announced that the final two weeks of the House session before the November midterm elections had been canceled, significantly shortening the full legislative calendar for September. House members are expected to leave Washington no later than September 17 and return no earlier than mid-November. The House will reconvene for another week of work after next week's Labor Day recess.
The compressed calendar has increased pressure on supporters of the sanctions legislation. Senior Republican aides said the bill remains a Republican priority, provided that Democrats "work it out." Democratic aides, responding to inquiries, expressed cautious optimism about the measure, while emphasizing uncertainty over whether Speaker Mike Johnson will bring it up for consideration.
"A good chance"
Vlasiuk said that during his visit to Washington, he held approximately 20 meetings with lawmakers and congressional staff, including discussions with members of both parties.
He said the Ukrainian delegation encountered broad support for increasing pressure on Russia, and that no lawmaker directly told him they would oppose the legislation.
Everyone agreed that pressure on Russia needed to be increased. No one said that they definitely would not support this bill
He described Ukraine as "quite optimistic" about the level of support for the legislation, particularly among Democrats.
One potentially important avenue could be for the House to consider the bill under a suspension of the rules - an expedited procedure typically used for bills expected to receive broad support. Vlasiuk said this was one of the realistic scenarios for advancing the bill.
I think there is a really good chance that this bill will be brought up for consideration
Vlasiuk had previously identified the week after next as Kyiv's preferred window for a vote in the House. Given the House's compressed calendar, this period could be one of the last opportunities for a vote before lawmakers leave Washington.
Asked whether momentum around the bill still existed, Vlasiuk pointed to what he characterized as continuing bipartisan support for Ukraine.
"There is a great deal of support for Ukraine on the Hill," he said, adding that Kyiv was emphasizing the urgency of passing the bill "very loudly." "At the same time, well, I mean, let's wait and see," Vlasiuk said.
Position on the tariff provisions
Vlasiuk defended the tariff provisions, arguing that they could make the sanctions significantly more effective. "This is a powerful tool that will make it possible to strengthen the effect of the sanctions," he said.
He argued that tariffs and sanctions may have a similar economic impact, but differ in how easily they can be circumvented.
"Sanctions can be adapted, sanctions can be circumvented. Tariffs cannot be adapted or circumvented," Vlasiuk said.
He also dismissed concerns that countries could be arbitrarily targeted by the bill, saying that the legislation establishes criteria based on purchases of Russian fossil fuels.
In particular, he pointed to China and India, which, as the publication writes, "Ukraine considers central to Russia’s continued ability to sell its energy exports."
Vlasiuk said the pressure could become a "huge blow" to Russia’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine also supports including Iran in the bill, he said, referring to Tehran’s close military cooperation with Moscow.
"Everyone understands how close the cooperation is between the military-industrial complexes of these countries," Vlasiuk said. "Therefore, Iran fully deserves to be recognized as such," he added.
For Kyiv, as noted, the urgency is not merely legislative.
Vlasiuk warned that Ukraine will face another difficult winter after months of Russian missile and drone attacks. He said that 160 people had been killed in missile and drone attacks in recent months.
"We must increase pressure on Russia to force it to change its plans, to force it to truly negotiate," he said.
He argued that passing the sanctions bill now would have two consequences: it could ultimately increase economic pressure on Russia, while immediately sending a political signal both to Ukraine and to the Russian government.
According to him, there is an element of inertia in sanctions policy. Even after the legislation is passed, implementing the measures could take several days, while a significant impact on Russia’s economy could take weeks.
"But at the same time, the very fact of passing this sanctions bill," Vlasiuk said, would send a "strong signal of support to the Ukrainian people" and a "truly strong signal to the Russian government."

articles.title: Iran uses BRICS judicial diplomacy to deepen ties with China, Russia and Belarus
articles.body:
Iran uses BRICS judicial diplomacy to deepen ties with China, Russia and Belarus
TEHRAN— Iran is seeking to turn judicial cooperation into a broader instrument of strategic diplomacy, with Judiciary Chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei holding talks with senior judicial officials from China, Russia and Belarus on the sidelines of the BRICS Chief Justices’ Forum in New Delhi.
The meetings, which brought together some of the highest-ranking judicial officials from the four countries, focused on legal cooperation, artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the exchange of judicial expertise. But they also carried a broader geopolitical message: Tehran says it intends to deepen its ties with major non-Western powers as the international system moves toward 'a new global order.'
The BRICS Chief Justices’ Forum, hosted by India’s Supreme Court from Sept. 4 to 6, is bringing together chief justices, presidents of supreme courts and senior judicial officials from BRICS members and partner countries. Its agenda includes international commercial disputes, cross-border enforcement of arbitration awards, artificial intelligence in judicial administration and sustainable development.
During a meeting with Zhang Jun, president of China’s Supreme People’s Court, Mohseni-Ejei said Tehran was determined to expand relations with Beijing and argued that stronger legal and judicial links could provide an institutional foundation for cooperation in wider strategic fields.
 
 “China and Iran have extensive and strong relations, and we are determined to expand our ties with China,” Mohseni-Ejei said, according to Iranian media.
He called for greater exchanges of legal expertise among BRICS members and urged the two countries to make fuller use of existing memoranda of understanding. He also singled out artificial intelligence and digital technologies as areas where Chinese experience could be combined with Iran’s domestic capabilities to open new avenues for cooperation.
Zhang welcomed the prospect of closer judicial ties, recalling his previous meeting with Mohseni-Ejei in China and describing their earlier discussions as deep and constructive. He said China and Iran had maintained stable relations despite regional and international upheavals and expressed hope that cooperation between the two countries would expand across a wider range of fields.
The emphasis on technology reflects the changing priorities of judicial institutions across the BRICS grouping. China, Zhang said, has been studying new approaches to judicial governance and the application of artificial intelligence and digital technologies, and is prepared to share those experiences with Iran.
For Tehran, such cooperation is not simply a technical matter. Mohseni-Ejei has repeatedly framed judicial and technological exchanges as part of a larger effort to strengthen ties among countries seeking greater independence from the existing Western-led international system.
 
  
A widening judicial network
Mohseni-Ejei also met Andrei Shved, chairman of Belarus’ Supreme Court, where the two sides discussed expanding judicial and legal cooperation.
The Iranian judiciary chief again highlighted artificial intelligence and technological exchanges, arguing that advances in digital tools could accelerate the handling of legal and judicial cases.
He said geopolitical developments had brought the international system to a historic turning point and suggested that cooperation among BRICS members and partner countries could help shape the emerging order.
Shved welcomed closer relations with Iran and invited Mohseni-Ejei to visit Belarus. He also said Minsk was prepared to work toward a new memorandum of understanding on judicial cooperation.
The Belarusian official said the two countries could use judicial ties as a channel for facilitating cooperation in other areas as well.
The meeting was part of a wider series of bilateral contacts taking place alongside the BRICS forum. India’s Supreme Court said judicial leaders from Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, together with partner countries including
Belarus, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, were participating in the three-day gathering.
Message to Washington
Alongside the legal and technological agenda, Mohseni-Ejei used his meetings to deliver a distinctly political assessment of Iran’s confrontation with the United States and Israel.
In a separate meeting with Igor Krasnov, chief justice of Russia’s Supreme Court, he said Iran and Russia could play a significant role in restoring regional and global stability through closer coordination and stronger strategic capabilities.
In remarks reported during his New Delhi meetings, Mohseni-Ejei said the United States and Israel had devoted their military and political resources to imposing an “unjust and illegal” war on Iran.
He maintained that Iran had withstood the pressure and that Washington had failed to accomplish its objectives.
“America is looking for a way out of the quagmire it has created for itself,” Mohseni-Ejei said, according to Iranian reports.
He argued that Iran’s ability to withstand the conflict had demonstrated Tehran's strategic resilience, while portraying closer cooperation with Russia, China and other non-Western powers as part of a broader response to changing global power dynamics.
The remarks come as Iranian officials increasingly present BRICS not merely as an economic grouping but as a platform through which Tehran can cultivate diplomatic, legal, technological and institutional relationships beyond traditional Western alliances.
Courts as instruments of wider diplomacy
The meetings in New Delhi also illustrate how judicial diplomacy is becoming intertwined with broader state-to-state relations.
Mohseni-Ejei told his Chinese counterpart that judicial cooperation could act as a “supporting arm” for strategic relations, suggesting that legal institutions can help create channels for cooperation in areas extending well beyond the courtroom.
That approach has particular significance for Iran, which faces extensive U.S. sanctions and has sought to deepen economic, political and technological ties with China and Russia while expanding relations with other members and partners of BRICS.
Artificial intelligence has emerged as one of the most practical areas for cooperation. The BRICS forum itself places AI and judicial administration among its central themes, alongside mediation, international commercial disputes, cross-border arbitration and sustainable development.
For Iran, the attraction is twofold: access to technological and institutional experience from countries such as China, while simultaneously strengthening links with a network of states that Tehran views as important to the emerging international balance.
Mohseni-Ejei has also expressed hope that Iran will eventually host a summit of the heads of judiciaries of Shanghai Cooperation Organization member states, further underscoring Tehran’s ambition to use judicial institutions as another channel of multilateral engagement.

articles.title: UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
Foreign fighters and support networks are fuelling the conflict in Sudan and worsening violence against civilians, a UN-backed investigation warned Thursday.
The United Nations' independent fact-finding mission on Sudan said foreign involvement was strengthening the military capabilities of the country's warring parties, enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations, with devastating consequences for ordinary people.
Since April 2023, the conflict between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and forced millions to flee their homes.
In a report, the probe documented the recruitment, training and deployment of foreign personnel to support the RSF, with transnational entities also facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, military technology and logistical support.
It also said there were reasonable grounds to believe that the regular army used foreign-supplied drones in its operations that harmed civilians and civilian infrastructure.
"This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians," said the fact-finding mission's chairman Mohamad Chande Othman.
"Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge."
The UN Human Rights Council established the probe in October 2023, to begin gathering evidence of violations in Sudan.
The independent investigative team does not speak on behalf of the United Nations.
Colombian contingent
The investigation documented the deployment of up to 2,000 ex-military Colombian contractors who directly operated combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units.
Witnesses also reported fighters from South Sudan, Chad and Ethiopia, "including women, serving primarily in frontline, rather than technical roles", identified by language, accent "and, in some cases uniforms", the report said.
Private entities, intermediaries and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit locations in Chad, Libya and Somalia to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons and logistics to the RSF in Sudan, the report said.
It found that foreign suppliers had boosted the RSF and the army's drone capabilities, allowing them to strike far beyond the front lines.
The mission found reasonable grounds to believe that the army and RSF attacks it documented may amount to war crimes.
Responding to the report, the United Arab Emirates insisted in a statement it was "not involved in the civil war in Sudan, nor has it provided arms or any related material to any party in Sudan since the outbreak of the conflict", and strongly condemned violations of international law by all sides.
The United States last month urged the UN Security Council to expand an arms embargo on the Darfur region to cover all of Sudan -- a call echoed by the fact-finding mission.
"Protecting Sudan's civilians requires action not only against those fighting the war, but also against the individuals, entities and networks that enable it to continue," said Chande Othman.

Iran-Russia alliance grows despite US pressure

Russia and Iran have significantly and systematically expanded their multifaceted cooperation in recent years, deepening their bonds across a wide and comprehensive range of vital areas, including bilateral trade, energy integration, strategic transportation corridors such as the International North–South Transport Corridor, and advanced defense cooperation. In the joint declaration, the leaders of the Eurasian powers denounced the military aggression as a flagrant violation of the fundamental principles and norms of international law, state sovereignty, and the United Nations Charter, warning that such reckless unilateral actions create grave, unprecedented risks to international peace, regional security, and global stability.
The SCO heads of state also officially expressed their sincere and deepest condolences on the assassination of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, who was martyred on the first day of the joint US-Israeli war on February 28. In his SCO meeting with Pezeshkian, Putin specifically asked the Iranian president to convey his warmest regards and words of sincere, unwavering support to Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, who was elected Leader of the Islamic Revolution following the assassination of his father.
Putin’s message of support to Iran’s new Leader is significant in this context. It suggests that Moscow’s backing for Tehran is rooted not in short-term political calculations, but in a broader strategic relationship that Russia is determined to maintain.

articles.title: A low-cost underwater drone was created specifically for Ukraine to strike Russian ships and bridges

A low-cost underwater drone was created specifically for Ukraine to strike Russian ships and bridges
Kyiv • UNN
A Danish company has developed an underwater drone with a 300-kg warhead for Ukraine. After testing in Denmark, it will be handed over to Ukraine.
Denmark has unveiled a new Shadowfin underwater maritime drone, developed by Søens Tech specifically to meet Ukraine’s needs for striking Russian ships and coastal infrastructure. Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
Shadowfin is 7 meters long, has a diameter of 50 centimeters, and a total weight of approximately 1.5 tons. The warhead accounts for 300 kg. The drone is also equipped with a mast featuring a GPS antenna and cameras, on which additional sensors can be installed.
One of the development’s main features is its price—approximately €50,000. Defense Express notes that this is cheaper than the cost of a Russian "Shahed", while the price of other unmanned boats and underwater maritime drones usually reaches hundreds of thousands of dollars.
The manufacturer lists enemy ships, ports, bridges, maritime terminals, and other coastal infrastructure facilities among Shadowfin’s potential targets. The low cost was achieved, in particular, thanks to its simple design—the drone’s hull is made from a standard 500-mm fiberglass pipe.
Shadowfin is currently undergoing testing in Danish waters. Once testing is complete, the company plans to transfer the first drone to Ukraine, where it will undergo field trials.

articles.title: Russia’s War Is Closing Its Own Skies as Airport Shutdowns Hit 993 in One Month
articles.body:

Russia’s War Is Closing Its Own Skies as Airport Shutdowns Hit 993 in One Month
Russia’s civilian aviation network suffered record disruption in August as Ukrainian drone operations repeatedly forced airports to suspend flights, with nearly 1,000 temporary closures recorded in a single month even before President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly declared Russian airspace increasingly unsafe.
According to The Wall Street Journal, citing aviation-security firm Osprey Flight Solutions, Russian airports were temporarily shut 993 times during August—more than a third above the July figure, WSJ reported on September 3.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On an average day, drone threats forced temporary restrictions at 32 airports across Russia, including major aviation hubs around Moscow and St. Petersburg.
The disruption over the summer has already surpassed the total recorded during all of last year.
From June through August, Russia experienced 2,182 temporary airport shutdowns. By comparison, 1,923 such cases were recorded throughout the entirety of 2025.
At the same time, Ukrainian drones are entering Russian-controlled airspace in unprecedented numbers.
Osprey estimated that around 16,000 Ukrainian drones crossed into Russian airspace in August, much of which Moscow continues to keep open to civilian aircraft.
Around 11,000 drones were recorded in June and more than 13,000 in July. Earlier in 2026, monthly totals generally remained between 4,000 and 5,000, apart from May, when the figure rose to 7,544.
The rising number of UAVs, combined with Russian air defenses attempting to intercept them and widespread GPS interference, is increasingly complicating civilian aviation.
Ukraine fully closed its own airspace to commercial traffic when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Moscow, by contrast, has kept most of Russia’s airspace open, restricting civilian flights primarily in regions closer to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy warned international airlines and insurers on September 1 that the risks of continuing to operate in Russian airspace were mounting.
“Although the Russian authorities do not report this as they should, the Russian sky will de facto be closed: the war unleashed by Russia is closing its sky,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that Ukraine does not target civilian aviation.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such—not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” the Ukrainian President stated.
Ukraine has also formally raised the issue with the International Civil Aviation Organization, arguing that Russia’s decision to keep civilian aircraft operating amid increasing military activity creates unnecessary risks.
Russian officials insist they will prevent major disruption.
“We are constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have solutions for all of this. We will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation,” Russian Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin said.
The operational figures, however, are moving in the opposite direction.
In the first three days of September alone, Russian airlines canceled an average of 86 flights per day, according to Flightradar24.
August exceeded that level on only two individual days—August 10, when 104 flights were canceled, and August 18, when 93 were called off.
Earlier, Turkey’s largest private airline, Pegasus Airlines, turned several Moscow-bound aircraft around mid-flight and canceled dozens of services to Russia overnight, amid drone-related disruptions at Russian airports and warnings from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the growing risks of operating in Russian airspace.
