articles.title: Civil rights groups campaign against deepening US-Israel defense cooperation
articles.body:
Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen US-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing US skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the US and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and US-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the US defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade. In a June letter to a US congressman, he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
US public support for Israel declines
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries, and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
US-Israel military aid agreement nears 2028 expiration
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028, and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto.

articles.title: Kuhestak mourns victims of deadly strike on wedding
articles.body:
Kuhestak mourns victims of deadly strike on wedding
TEHRAN- The wedding was supposed to be a night of music, laughter and celebration. Instead, the people of this small coastal town gathered on Thursday to carry coffins through the streets, mourning those killed when a house hosting a wedding celebration was struck during the latest escalation of the US-Iran conflict.
The funeral procession for the victims began on the main boulevard at the entrance to Kuhestak, in Sirik County in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province. Families of the dead, local residents, religious figures and officials walked together toward the town’s cemetery, turning what should have been a celebration of a new marriage into a day of collective mourning.
Among the coffins was a small one belonging to Amir Mohammad Karimi, a four-year-old boy whose death has become the most haunting image of the tragedy.
Photographs and videos circulating on Iranian social media showed mourners gathering around the child’s coffin, with his name and age repeatedly appearing in posts about the attack. Iranian media described the burial of Amir Mohammad as one of the most painful moments of the funeral.
He was four years old.
That fact has come to define the grief in Kuhestak: a child who had no part in the conflict, killed on a night when families had gathered for a wedding.
The procession brought together people from across the local community, including families of the victims and both Shiite and Sunni religious leaders. Their presence reflected the close-knit character of the coastal communities of Sirik, where religious and family ties are deeply woven into daily life.
The scene was starkly different from what the house had been only hours earlier. The gathering had been a wedding celebration, with relatives and friends assembled together. Then came the explosion.
The United States has said its strikes in the area were aimed at military assets, including air-defense systems, radar installations, maritime equipment, mine-laying capabilities and communications facilities. Washington has also said it does not intentionally target civilians and has launched an investigation into what happened at the wedding site.
But an analysis by Reuters has added weight to the Iranian account of what happened. Weapons experts examining verified images and videos from the scene concluded that the destruction was likely caused by a direct hit from a US munition, rather than by a ricochet or another form of indirect damage. One expert assessed that the weapon was likely a 500-pound air-dropped bomb.
For the people of Kuhestak, however, the question of military targeting has been overtaken by the human cost.
On Thursday, the town’s streets were filled not with wedding guests but mourners. Coffins were carried through the entrance boulevard as people gathered along the route. Images from the funeral captured scenes of men carrying the dead, relatives grieving and crowds accompanying the victims to their final resting place.
And amid the adults stood the memory of a little boy.
Amir Mohammad’s name appeared repeatedly across Iranian social media in the aftermath of the attack. Images of his funeral and burial were shared widely, with users focusing on the unbearable contrast between his age and the circumstances of his death.
His coffin was small enough to be carried easily. The grief surrounding it was not.
The tragedy has also revived wider concerns over civilian casualties in the US-Iran conflict. Reuters reported that the strike killed five civilians, including a four-year-old child, and injured nearly 70 people. The incident drew particular attention because the victims were attending a private family celebration rather than a military gathering.
For Kuhestak, the memory of Sept. 1 is now inseparable from the image of a wedding interrupted by war.
A celebration meant to mark the beginning of a marriage ended with families searching for the wounded and counting their dead. Two days later, the town gathered again — this time not to celebrate a new beginning, but to say farewell.

articles.title: Czechia issues warning over Russia-linked attempts to access Signal accounts
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
The Czech Republic’s cybersecurity watchdog has warned of attempts by actors primarily linked to Russia to gain access to accounts on the encrypted messaging application Signal, local media reported on Friday.
The National Cyber and Information Security Agency said the attacks mainly target politicians, government officials and security experts, though any user could fall victim, Radio Prague International reported.
According to the agency, the attackers do not seek to breach Signal’s encryption. Instead, they use social engineering techniques to persuade users to connect an unknown device to their account or disclose their personal identification number.
The methods include fraudulent messages purporting to come from Signal’s support service, malicious links and fake QR codes disguised as invitations to join groups, it added.
By convincing users to link another device to their accounts, attackers can gain unauthorized access without directly compromising the application’s encryption.
The agency urged users to remain cautious when receiving unsolicited messages, links or QR codes and to verify requests before linking new devices to their accounts.
The warning follows similar campaigns reported earlier this year in the Netherlands, Germany, Ukraine and other European countries.
In March, the Netherlands’ AIVD and MIVD intelligence services warned of what they described as a large-scale global campaign by Russian state actors targeting government employees, military personnel, civil servants and journalists.
In April, German authorities also warned of attacks targeting senior politicians, lawmakers, diplomats, military officers and journalists. Berlin later said it believed Russia was behind the campaign, while federal prosecutors opened an espionage investigation.

articles.title: Jaishankar says India in touch with Russia, Ukraine to help end war
articles.body:
File photo: Minister of external affairs S Jaishankar
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Friday said India has been in continuous touch with both Ukraine and Russia and is exploring whether ideas and suggestions can be developed to contribute to the mitigation and, ideally, the cessation of the conflict.Jaishankar made the remarks in Warsaw after holding talks with Poland's deputy Prime Minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, a day after he met the top Ukrainian leadership in Kyiv.
‘Endless war must give way to an end to war’
Addressing a joint press meet with Sikorski, Jaishankar said the two leaders discussed major global and regional issues, including the war in Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year.“The deputy Prime Minister and I also understandably discussed some major global and regional issues, notable among them is the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year... I myself have just come here from Kyiv,” he said.
Replying to a question, Jaishankar said India remained in touch with both sides.“What we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they will contribute to the mitigation, ideally, the cessation of the conflict,” he added.Jaishankar reiterated India's position that the conflict must end through dialogue and diplomacy.
“India believes that endless war must give way to an end to war. These are wars without winners. Every additional day means more death, more destruction, more loss to the parties themselves, and more cost to the rest of the world,” he said.
“Our efforts must therefore focus on promoting dialogue and diplomacy. We must each do what we can in whichever way we believe could be most effective and support the efforts of others to bring this conflict to an end. This is India's strong conviction, and we are acting on it,” he added.
Jaishankar rejects trade link to ending war
Responding to a question on India's purchases of Russian oil, Jaishankar said the solution to the conflict lay in negotiations rather than trade.“This war is not going to end... not because somebody chose to buy or not buy oil or alumina or fertilisers or metals and minerals. It will end when there is diplomacy, when there is dialogue and when there is negotiation. So, I think let's diagnose the problem right,” he said.A day earlier in Kyiv, Jaishankar had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and foreign minister Andrii Sybiha and said India was ready to extend “any help in any manner” to help end the war.Following the meeting, Zelenskyy said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

Jaishankar and Sikorski also discussed complex global challenges, including supply chain resilience and food, fuel and fertiliser security.The two ministers reviewed the progress of the India-Poland Joint Action Plan 2024-28, covering areas including trade and investment, space, digital technology, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, defence, education, shipping, mining and energy.Jaishankar also called on Polish President Karol Nawrocki and discussed the trajectory of the India-Poland Strategic Partnership, as well as the Ukraine conflict and developments in West Asia.

In an evening video address, Zelenskyy said his country received details on Witkoff and Kushner’s schedule from the American side and that the Ukrainian side is preparing for the envoys’ visit to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy expressed that Kyiv will not be launching strikes over the course of Witkoff and Kushner’s visit to Russia, and called on Moscow to take mirror steps in this context when the envoys arrive in Ukraine.
“Our goal is the most constructive, meaningful visit and negotiations with the American side. We need to look for real options to bring this war to an end. We'll see what proposals Steve and Jared have and what Moscow will say to them,” Zelenskyy added.
Earlier Friday, the Axios news website and Russian state news agency Tass reported, citing sources, that the two US envoys will visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
Witkoff and Kushner have never visited Kyiv, while both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began. Their latest visit was on Jan. 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.

Ukraine does not expect conditions for a ceasefire with Russia to emerge before spring 2027, Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov said.
Citing an interview with Budanov last weekend, The New York Times reported Friday that he believes conditions for a halt to hostilities in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war are unlikely to emerge before spring.
“Negotiations will sooner or later come to something. You cannot fight your whole life,” Budanov was quoted as saying.
His remarks came a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an evening video address that Kyiv hopes to meet US President Donald Trump’s envoys “in the coming days.”
Zelenskyy said there are “preliminary dates” for a visit by US envoys to the Ukrainian capital and that Kyiv expects to receive the representatives. The envoys are also expected to hold meetings in Moscow.
Moscow and Kyiv last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks on Jan. 23-24, Feb. 4-5 and Feb. 17-18. The first two rounds were held in Abu Dhabi, while the third took place in Geneva.
The negotiations have since been paused, with Moscow and Kyiv attributing the halt to Washington’s focus on Iran following the outbreak of war in late February.
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner have never visited Kyiv, while both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began. Their latest visit was on Jan. 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.
Citing sources, news website Axios and Russian state news agency Tass reported earlier Friday that the two US envoys are expected to visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

articles.title: Who Is Adam Telle, Trump’s New Acting Army Secretary?
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that Adam Telle, the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works, will temporarily replace Dan Driscoll as the Army’s top civilian leader following Driscoll’s abrupt resignation from the role earlier this week.
Trump lauded Telle as "a Great Patriot, who is respected by all” in a Truth Social post, saying Telle would take over as acting Army Secretary “effective immediately.”
The news comes after Driscoll, who Trump nominated as Army Secretary last year after returning to the White House, stepped down amid reports of tension between him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Hegseth praised Trump’s announcement on Thursday, calling Telle “strong and whip smart.”
“Huge congrats to Adam,” Hegseth said in a post on X. “He is indeed a great Patriot — and will be an immediate asset to the @USArmy.”
Here’s what to know about Telle.
Telle has overseen the Army Corps of Engineers since last year
Telle was sworn into his current role as the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works last August, becoming the second person nominated by the President to an Army position in Trump's second term to be confirmed by the Senate, according to Telle's biography on the U.S. military’s website.
In that position, Telle has served as a civilian official in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, an agency that builds and maintains infrastructure, including dams. According to his bio, he has had “principal authority to establish policy direction and to provide supervision of all aspects” of the civil works tasks that the agency performs for the Army, including projects aimed at reducing flood and storm damage.
Telle previously worked under multiple Republican senators
Before being appointed to his current role in the Trump Administration, Telle served as the chief of staff to Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty of Tennessee from 2021-2025, according to Legistorm. He previously worked under another Republican, then-Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi, for about a decade from 2007-2017, and held various roles in the office, including deputy chief of staff and legislative director, according to Legistorm. While serving in Cochran’s office, he helped with the lawmaker’s work on Hurricane Katrina recovery, according to his Army bio.
Telle also served on the Senate Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee that was responsible for overseeing the Department of Homeland Security’s budget, according to his bio.
Telle served in the first Trump Administration
During Trump’s first term in the Oval Office, Telle served on the White House Office of Legislative Affairs’ Senate team and “was President Trump’s chief liaison to the Senate,” according to his Army bio.
Telle will take over as acting Army Secretary at a tumultuous time
Telle will step into his new role in the Army at a time of turmoil both abroad and within the Department of Defense.
The war in Iran, which began on Feb. 28, has now stretched on for longer than six months and has sparked backlash from many Americans.
And Telle will also be taking on the new position amid upheaval within the U.S. military’s senior ranks. About 20 military and civilian leaders have been ousted or have resigned since Hegseth took over the Department of Defense, including Driscoll earlier this week. Even some Republicans have criticized Hegseth for the chaos at the agency, including Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who has called on Trump to replace the Defense Secretary.
“[Hegseth] is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” Tillis said in a social media post this week. “I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

articles.title: Guard F-16s Kept Pace on Kadena Deployment, but Edge Wears Thin
articles.body:
An F-16 Air National Guard unit’s six-month deployment to Kadena Air Base, Japan, this year illustrated the capabilities the Guard’s oldest fighter units can still offer—but also the challenges they face, officials told reporters this week.
On one hand, leaders said the Colorado ANG’s 120th Fighter Squadron was largely able to keep pace with its fifth-generation teammates and hone its Agile Combat Employment skills throughout the Pacific.
But on the other, the squadron’s 1980s-era F-16s are starting to show their age and lack at least some of the high-end capabilities the Air Force has said it wants to prioritize for a high-end fight.
“We’re able to keep up, with the exception of obviously being a fourth‑gen airplane,” Lt. Col. Frank “Chester” Prokop, squadron commander and detachment commander during the deployment, said. “We can’t get nearly as close to surface‑to‑air threats or air‑to‑air threats posed by China over there as some of the newer models. So, we’re kind of getting to the end of our capability. We’ve maxed it out. We played the perfect game.”
The January-to-June deployment, part of a rotation of fighters through Kadena as the base waits for its new F-15EX Eagle IIs, is a signpost of things to come for both the Air Force’s total fighter fleet, but more specifically for challenges faced inside the Air National Guard. The fleet is getting older while replacements are slowly ordered and delivered, and with the Active-Duty force being prioritized, the Guard is pushing the envelope with its legacy aircraft.
“The first piece is that any aging airframe is going to negatively impact operational availability and daily ops tempo,” Heather Penney, a former F-16 fighter pilot who now serves as the director of studies and research at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “I mean, you could talk about taking your 35‑year‑old car to an F1 race. Is that really what you want to do?”
Six Months at Kadena
Originally, the 120th was supposed to deploy a dozen of its F-16C Block 30 jets to Kadena from January to May. But that stay was extended six weeks due to demands across the Air Force related to Operation Epic Fury and the conflict with Iran. The conflict also impacted plans to join exercises in Thailand.
Still, the Guardsmen and their jets got to put into practice the Agile Combat Employment training they—with the rest of the Air Force—have been putting in for years now. ACE envisions small teams of Airmen dispersing from large central hubs to operate from remote or austere airfields, and the 120th implemented that through “small-package movements,” shuffling two to six jets around the region.
Prokop and 140th Wing Command Col. Christopher “KojaCk” Melka said the unit can now generate detailed ACE deployment packages, including personnel, aircraft load, and ground equipment needs, in 10-15 minutes, rather than the weeklong planning cycles common only a few years ago.
For a Philippines deployment, the squadron took four F-16s with a C-130 and worked with Marine Corps units. For Exercise Beverly Midnight at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, Japan, the unit conducted hot-pit refueling and rearming work alongside F-35s.
The unit also employed the “Multi-Capable Airman” approach to shrink its maintenance manpower footprint, Melka said. Operating mostly out of Kadena, a smaller package of cross-trained airmen handled various maintenance tasks for the squadron, rather than relying on a larger footprint with specialized technicians.
“We’ve actually exposed some of our Airmen to other career fields to give them a little bit more background on both, so that if, for whatever reason, they found themselves in a more austere environment where we could only send a certain package of maintainers and support personnel, maybe one person covered the duties of two,” Melka said.
Recap Ripple Effects
While the 120th was able to practice concepts like Agile Combat Employment and Multi-Capable Airmen during its deployment, the unit also had to stretch to keep its F-16s going, Melka and Prokop said.
“When these F-16s were first produced, it was roughly about six to eight maintenance man-hours per flight hour,” Prokop said. “Now, our maintainers are averaging 15 to 20 maintenance man-hours for every hour of flight.”
That’s because issues that require more in-depth maintenance, such as structural failures such as cracks on the airframe, “are happening at a much increasing rate right now,” Prokop said. “And that is probably the biggest challenge that we face is our maintenance unit has not received any increase in manpower commensurate with the level of increased requirements for maintenance time on the aircraft.”
The unit has been fortunate, the lieutenant colonel said, to have experienced, veteran maintainers working those airframes. But the increased maintenance needs are pushing leadership to make adjustments, like using more simulator flight time rather than flying hours to keep pilots sharp.
“The capacity of our maintainers to keep them safe and keep them combat effective is still working very well,” Melka said.
The jets themselves have also been upgraded many times over the years to stay effective with things like new AESA radars, Link 16 data links, and ongoing software upgrades; Prokop noted the F-16 has an unofficial nickname of the “Burger King jet” as a reference to the fast-food chain’s “Have It Your Way” slogan.
Nevertheless, the decades-old aircraft, while competent now, are closer to the end of their service lives—and the 120th is one of around a dozen Guard squadrons that have not been officially selected to recapitalize their fleets with newer aircraft such as the F-35A or F-15EX, leaving the unit’s future in doubt.
For now, Penney said, units like the 120th can keep flying their F-16s. But the Air Force has yet to signal its long-term plan for them and currently isn’t buying new jets fast enough to replace the older jets anytime soon.
“The Air Force has got to recapitalize at a meaningful rate, because they have deferred and delayed increasing their recapitalization rate,” Penney said. “If you want to be recapitalized by 2035, you’ve got to buy more than 100 fighters a year.”
Service leaders have said they need to procure at least 72 fighters per year to keep the fleet’s age from increasing. But the last time the service managed to budget for that was in fiscal 2024.
In fiscal 2025, the budget request was for 60 fighters. In 2026, it dropped to a low of 45. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending, is for just 62 fighters.
And even then, these new fighters—the F-35 and F-15EX—are mostly going to the Active-Duty force, leaving the Guard to wait. That could have a ripple effect, as the Guard deploys in nearly any major contingency or large-scale operation as a need, not an add-on, Penney said.
“If the Air Force does not recapitalize the Guard in a concurrent and proportional manner, they risk not only losing a key element of the total force, but they risk leaving the Guard with operationally irrelevant airframes,” Penney said.

articles.title: US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
articles.body:
US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
WASHINGTON – US military officials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Sept 4 by US Senator Ron Wyden and statements given to Reuters, a development that follows reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.
The Air Force told Wyden that it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two months ago.
US Special Operations Command said in a separate letter that it had “recently” disabled them on its Windows devices.
The Army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier in 2026.
Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue for months.
The disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers – companies that collate and resell personal data – can be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.
The Air Force and Special Operations Command declined further comment.
Similar letters from the Army and Navy to Wyden said they disabled advertising IDs on military devices but gave no indication of when the restrictions were imposed.
The Army said in a statement that advertising IDs had been blocked on Windows computers “since before 2021” but that Android and Apple mobile devices had only had it disabled by default “since at least February 2026”.
Messages seeking comment from the Navy went unreturned.
The effort to reduce the location data generated by smartphones comes as military officials weigh increasingly strict restrictions on phone use overall.
In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting to the internet were helping Iran target American bases in the region.
Wyden and US Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, sent a letter to the Pentagon on Sept 4 asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade.
The letter included the updates from the various service branches on their efforts to disable advertising IDs on military devices.
Wyden said in a statement that it was clear that the military’s efforts “have not been effective at neutralising this threat”. Harrigan said that US enemies “should not be able to pull out a credit card and buy information that helps them track American troops”.
The Pentagon said in an e-mail it would respond to the lawmakers directly.
Mobile advertising IDs, often abbreviated MAID, are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that can be used to track a person’s activity across mobile apps and pinpoint their physical location.
Zach Edwards, co-founder of privacy ad tech company Decryptads, said that efforts to disable MAID on military-operated devices were “definitely a positive thing”.
The restrictions “will essentially ensure their location isn’t being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors”, although he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other more complicated ways, for example by triangulating technical device details with network data or location information. articles.title: Israeli-backed militia kills Islamic Jihad member in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli-backed militia kills PIJ member in Gaza amid string of attacks by Tel Aviv's proxy forces
An Israeli-backed Palestinian militia killed a member of the Al-Quds Brigades, the armed wing of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), on Friday during an attempt to abduct him in al-Qarara, north of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, according to the group.
In a press statement, the Al-Quds Brigades said a militia force advanced towards al-Qarara at dawn, with support from Israeli drones, in an attempt to abduct one of its members.
The Al-Quds Brigades said its fighters detected the force and engaged it with grenades and medium weapons at close range.
Several militia members were killed or wounded before Israeli drones intervened to cover their withdrawal, according to the group.
The drones then allegedly killed Fadi al-Abadla, a member of the Al-Qarara Battalion of the Khan Younis Brigade, leaving his body at the scene, according to the statement. The militia withdrew with its dead and wounded.
There was no immediate comment from the Israeli military or the alleged militia.
Separately, speaking with The New Arab, local residents in Khan Younis said they heard gunfire and clashes in al-Qarara during the early morning, coinciding with the presence of Israeli drones.
One eyewitness said the area had recently seen a growing presence of armed groups, while residents were unable to identify the force or determine its objective.
The incident came two days after Moen al-Arabeed, head of Hamas's internal security apparatus in Gaza, was abducted from Gaza City.
Palestinian sources initially suggested Israeli-backed militias were responsible, but Hamas sources later said an Israeli special forces unit had carried out the operation directly.
The two incidents have brought renewed attention to the activities of Palestinian armed groups reportedly operating with Israeli support.
Israel's Palestinian proxies
An investigation published by Haaretz in late August, based on testimonies from Israeli soldiers and officers, satellite imagery and conversations with Gaza residents, identified five-armed militias operating at six locations across the Strip and receiving Israeli financial and military support.
According to the investigation, the Israeli army and Shin Bet maintain close coordination with the groups, which are primarily hostile to Hamas.
An Israeli Air Force officer quoted by Haaretz said the government, army and Shin Bet send armed and trained militias into Gaza to carry out security missions, while the Air Force is instructed to protect them during their operations.
The groups are tasked with pursuing Hamas and other Palestinian faction members, conducting raids and kidnappings, gathering intelligence and operating in areas where Israeli forces face difficulties moving directly, according to Haaretz.
They have also been accused of attacking Palestinian civilians, looting property and burning homes, as well as participating in efforts to drive residents from certain areas.
The Yasser Abu Shabab group has emerged as one of the most prominent of these formations. It operated mainly in southern Gaza, particularly Rafah, and openly acknowledged cooperation with Israel.
In July 2025, Abu Shabab told an Israeli television channel that his group received support from the Israeli military.
Despite Abu Shabab's subsequent death under unclear circumstances, Haaretz reported that Israel's militia strategy continued to develop, particularly following the October 2025 ceasefire.
The groups do not appear capable of replacing the Israeli military or independently controlling Gaza. Instead, their role appears focused on specific security and intelligence operations, allowing Israel to use local Palestinian actors against its opponents.
'Tools of Israel'
Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA that Israel's reliance on the militias forms part of a strategy to create local Palestinian forces capable of carrying out operations inside Gaza.
"The militias cannot be regarded as independent Palestinian forces given their Israeli funding, weapons and operational coordination," he said.
He warned that their expansion could deepen Palestinian divisions by shifting confrontation towards armed clashes between Palestinian groups.
Akram Attallah, a political analyst in Gaza, told TNA that the militias are "tools of Israel […] Tel Aviv uses them when it wants to conduct operations indirectly but deploys its own forces when an operation exceeds their capabilities".
Attallah said the abduction of Moen al-Arabeed demonstrated the overlap between direct Israeli military operations and those carried out through locally backed armed groups.
He added that Israel can shift between using Palestinian proxies and deploying its own forces depending on an operation's nature and scale, making the distinction between the militias and the Israeli military increasingly difficult to separate.
For Attallah, the development of these groups reflects a broader Israeli effort to create Palestinian actors capable of performing security functions inside Gaza, potentially reshaping the Strip's security landscape and deepening divisions between Palestinian factions.

articles.title: Dreadnought supplier contract ended after security reviews
articles.body:
A contract within the supply chain for Britain’s new Dreadnought-class nuclear ballistic missile submarines was terminated following security reviews by the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, the Ministry of Defence has confirmed.
The disclosure came in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked the Defence Secretary about a “fruitless payment” associated with the Dreadnought supply chain recorded in the MOD’s Annual Report and Accounts for 2025-26.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard replied: “A contract within the Dreadnought supply chain was terminated following security reviews by the Defence Nuclear Enterprise. The detail is unsuitable for disclosure due to the classification and sensitivity of the programme.”
The answer does not identify the contractor, of course, or the part of the Dreadnought programme affected or the circumstances which led the Defence Nuclear Enterprise to terminate the agreement.
The reference to a fruitless payment comes from the MOD’s annual accounts. Such payments are recorded in government accounts where expenditure has been incurred without the intended benefit being received, although Pollard’s answer does not provide the value or nature of the payment associated with this particular case.
The Dreadnought programme is delivering the four submarines intended to replace the Royal Navy’s existing Vanguard-class boats and carry the UK’s submarine-launched nuclear deterrent. Construction is centred at BAE Systems’ submarine shipyard in Barrow-in-Furness, supported by a large industrial and nuclear supply chain across the country.
The programme sits within the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise, which covers the organisations, infrastructure, personnel and industrial capacity needed to support Britain’s nuclear deterrent. Security controls around the enterprise are correspondingly stringent, with detailed information on individual suppliers and sensitive components often withheld.
The first Dreadnought-class submarine, HMS Dreadnought, is being built alongside the other boats in the class as the Royal Navy prepares to transition from Vanguard while maintaining continuous at-sea deterrence.

articles.title: USAF Tests C2 Capabilities Across 4,000 Miles in High-Stress Virtual Exercise
articles.body:
The Air Force recently conducted a virtual stress test of its command-and-control capabilities, linking Air Operations Centers in New Mexico and the United Kingdom and forcing commanders to run personnel recovery and strikes under simulated fire.
Between Aug. 4-7, the 705th Combat Training Squadron at Kirtland Air Force Base, N.M., hosted Virtual Flag 26-4, which included more than 267 participants from the Air Force, Space Force, Army, Marine Corps, United Kingdom, and Australia.
“The foundation of joint warfighting is built in exercises like Virtual Flag,” Col. James Fields II, commander of the 505th Command and Control Wing, said in a release. “This event is where we prove that we are the Air Force’s premier organization for operational command and control.”
The 505th, headquartered at Hurlburt Field, Fla., with units scattered across the country, served as the operational “hub” for the exercise as participants trained in a distributed, contested environment using joint and coalition C2.
The exercise focused on creating “realistic friction” between the tactical and operational levels of C2, according to the release.
Another focus for the exercise was delivering a complete intelligence picture for commanders. Marine Corps Air Squadron 1 and Marine Air Control Squadron 2, both out of Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, N.C., tied together all the intel streams to provide a common tactical picture for all commanders, serving as a multifunction air operations center.
“They provided the critical expertise needed to ensure every single participant, from our pilots in the virtual simulators to our commanders in the [Air Operations Center], was looking at the exact same, accurate common tactical picture,” McCarthy said. “That shared view of the battlespace is the absolute foundation of joint C2.”
Realistic Training
To provide realistic intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance simulations, the exercise brought in new participants.
VF 26-4 was the first to have crews for MQ-9 Reaper drones and RC-135 Rivet Joints participate, rather than relying on traditional “white carding” of their capabilities. The exercise also simulated capabilities for the E-3 Sentry and E-7 Wedgetail for airborne early warning and control.
“In a peer conflict, identifying tracks and targets is going to require a robust ISR enterprise,” Maj. James McCarthy, director of operations for the 705th, said. “This is extremely valuable because it helps our C2 community understand what the ISR enterprise can and cannot provide in a high-tempo fight.”
The exercise practiced dispersed operations between the main base at Kirtland’s Distributed Mission Operations Center and the “forward” base, the Royal Air Battlespace Training Centre, at RAF Waddington, England, more than 4,000 miles away.
“That connectivity is important because it enables operational command and control training across geographically separated teams, helping warfighters practice the coordination, communication and decision-making required in real-world joint and coalition operations,” Lt. Col. Sajjad Abdullateef, 705th Combat Training Squadron commander, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a written statement.
The inclusion of Australian and British forces was important, retired USAF Col. George Dougherty told Air & Space Forces Magazine; most allied partners have historically let the United States take the lead in developing network architecture, tech, and standards for C2 systems.
“The U.S. was way ahead in terms of real-time battle management C2,” said Dougherty, who served as assistant to the Air Force’s program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management. “Europe/NATO was, for instance, more focused on strategic and collective ministerial-level C2, which is a bigger challenge for their collective multinational decision-making and planning.”
A Balancing Act
As commanders worked through their AOCs receiving simulated strikes, launching aircraft for reconnaissance and personnel recovery, they had to move units and platforms around the virtual battlespace, which affects sortie generation, sustainment, and mission planning, Abdullateef wrote.
“Commanders were required to balance survivability against mission effectiveness,” Abdullateef wrote. “They had to determine how and where to disperse forces, how to continue supporting the daily Air Tasking Order despite personnel and resource losses, and how to preserve combat power for follow-on operations.”
Operational C2 requires commanders and their staffs to translate shared understanding into timely decisions, synchronized actions, and combat effects across distributed forces, Abdullateef wrote.
“Stepping into a Wing Operations Center to manage six mission generation force elements across three simulated bases is a massive departure from our Airmen’s daily tactical routines, and Virtual Flag 26-4 provided the proving ground,” said an Air Force major serving as the exercise deputy offensive director.
“What started as an uncomfortable learning curve quickly turned into operational confidence as our team synchronized our offensive and defensive sections from home station,” the major said. “They streamlined our internal reporting, integrated real-time logistics and base defense with sortie generation, and proved our forces are ready to execute distributed command and control under contested conditions.”
Virtual Yet Real Enough
Though the virtual exercise didn’t provide live-fire experience, the simulated nature of the event gave participants experience they could not have gained in a standard, smaller-scale live-fire event.
“The virtual environment allows us to provide high-quality, high-repetition training in a fiscally responsible manner,” said Wing Commander Richard Kinniburgh, a Royal Air Force exchange officer with the 505th Test and Training Group. “More importantly, it allows us to present our warfighters with a scale of conflict that would be impossible to replicate in a live-fly exercise. We also remove many of the real-world friction points that can cancel live-fly training, ensuring our warfighters get the maximum training value out of every event.”
As this edition Virtual Flag wrapped, planners and operators pull in the lessons learned for future iterations of the exercise and to better inform the Air Force-wide C2 community.
“That matters because the value of Virtual Flag is not just executing the event,” Abdullateef wrote. “It is learning how decisions affected the broader force, identifying what worked and what required adjustment, and using that feedback to strengthen future operational C2 training.”

Russian Ballistic Missiles Destroy Warehouse Holding Ai Weiwei Artwork Near Kyiv
A warehouse housing an installation by internationally renowned Chinese artist Ai Weiwei was destroyed during a Russian missile attack on the Kyiv region on July 19, the artist said.
He stated that the warehouse, located in the Bucha district on the outskirts of Kyiv, was hit by two ballistic missiles during the Russian attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The facility contained Ai’s installation Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White. The extent of the damage to the artwork itself remains unclear.
World-renowned Chinese dissident artist and sculptor Ai Weiwei presented his first major installation in Ukraine in fall 2025. Titled Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White, the work explores themes of war and concealment, as well as the tension between ideals of rational order and the realities of contemporary war.
Created specifically for its presentation in Ukraine, the installation was unveiled at Pavilion 13, a multidisciplinary cultural venue. The work reflects Ai’s longstanding humanist and pacifist perspective, shaped by his experiences with state repression and his broader artistic exploration of violence, displacement, and political power.
Ai Weiwei is widely regarded as one of the most prominent figures in contemporary art, combining artistic practice with outspoken criticism of authoritarianism and political repression.
His work has been exhibited at major international events and institutions, including the Venice Biennale, Documenta, and the São Paulo Biennial. Ai’s personal history has also been shaped by persecution by the Chinese authorities, beginning with the targeting of his family.
The reported destruction of the warehouse comes as Ukraine’s cultural sector continues to document the impact of Russia’s war on art and cultural heritage.
In May, an exhibition highlighting the work of photographers and documentary creators covering war and its human consequences under extreme conditions opened at the Cannes Film Festival, according to the Ukrainian Association of Professional Photographers.

articles.title: US Commander Reveals What Really Happened When His Bradleys Faced Ukraine’s Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- World
US Commander Reveals What Really Happened When His Bradleys Faced Ukraine’s Drones
A US Army Bradley company spent 10 days being watched, hunted and forced to rethink how it moved under drones operated by Ukrainian troops with real combat experience—before those same Ukrainians switched sides and began teaching the Americans how drone warfare is actually fought.
Blackhawk Company of the US Army’s 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment trained alongside Ukraine’s 412th Nemesis Unmanned Systems Brigade during the Combined Resolve exercise at the Hohenfels training area in Germany.
The commander of Blackhawk Company later challenged portrayals of the exercise as a simple rout of US armor by Ukrainian drones, writing in Task & Purpose on September 3 that such accounts did not fully capture either his unit’s performance or the lessons American soldiers took away from the training.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The two units had already met before the active phase began, giving American troops an early introduction to Ukrainian drone operators whose tactics had been shaped by years of battlefield experience during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
Once the exercise began, however, that experience became an immediate problem for the US mechanized force, the commander wrote.
Blackhawk Company entered the training area in a column of Bradley infantry fighting vehicles through a limited access point. Ukrainian reconnaissance drones were already overhead, watching the formation as it moved into the battlespace.
The American company did not have some of the newer counter-drone equipment currently being tested by the US Army, leaving its troops to operate while knowing that hostile aerial reconnaissance could track their movements.
That forced a rapid change in tactics.
Rather than concentrate vehicles and personnel in familiar formations, the Americans began spreading them as widely as possible. Bradleys were hidden beneath heavy tree cover, while crews became increasingly conscious of how their vehicles appeared from above rather than focusing solely on threats visible from ground level. Movement also changed.
Instead of relying on roads and trails that drone operators could easily monitor, the mechanized company began using steep gullies, valleys and difficult terrain to conceal its movements.
That sometimes meant sending heavy Bradleys across slopes and terrain that mechanized units would normally prefer to avoid. Natural cover and dead ground helped reduce exposure to Ukrainian reconnaissance systems and made the company less predictable from the air.
The exercise still produced simulated losses of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles, but the American commander argued that this did not make heavy armor obsolete.
Bradleys and Abrams tanks continued protecting their crews and allowed soldiers to move rapidly through difficult terrain while pursuing their objectives. The lesson, in his account, was not to abandon armor but to change how armored formations operate when drones can observe almost every conventional movement.
According to the commander of Blackhawk Company, the most valuable phase came later. During the second half of Combined Resolve, Nemesis stopped operating against Blackhawk Company and joined the US troops for offensive operations.
That allowed the Americans to observe Ukrainian drone warfare from the other side.
Nemesis operators demonstrated techniques developed through combat in Ukraine, including methods for flying inexpensive drones over surprisingly long distances and rapidly moving targeting information from sensors to weapons.
For US troops, the Ukrainian approach provided a practical lesson in shortening the sensor-to-shooter chain—the process of detecting a target, identifying it, passing its location to a weapon system and engaging it before the target can move.
The Americans left the exercise with techniques they could incorporate into their own formations, while the experience also reinforced a less technological lesson.
Earlier, reports emerged that German Leopard 2 units were beginning to apply battlefield lessons from Ukraine, fitting tanks with new protective netting designed to reduce their vulnerability to drone attacks.
The changes were visible in photographs released by the Bundeswehr from Exercise Freedom Shield 2026, held at the Pabradė training area in Lithuania from June 6 to 19.

articles.title: Qatari ITU submission confirms Iran’s retaliatory operations hit only US military assets
articles.body:
Qatari ITU submission confirms Iran’s retaliatory operations hit only US military assets
TEHRAN — Official documentation submitted by Doha to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) validates that Iran’s recent defensive measures aimed exclusively at American military infrastructure on Qatari soil, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei.
In a statement published on X on Thursday, Baghaei referenced Qatar’s official contribution to an extraordinary session of the ITU Council. The safety and security risk assessment report explicitly noted that Iran’s strikes “were directed towards US military facilities. […] No civilian areas have been targeted.”
The document further specified that “almost all of the attacks were directed towards US military facilities, with the one exception of an attack against the gas facilities at Ras Laffan on 18th March,” while evaluating the current security risk to Qatar as minimal.
Addressing the sole exception mentioned in the report, Baghaei provided necessary context regarding the targeted energy infrastructure: “It should be recalled, however, that the facilities struck that day were serving US military aggression against Iran.”
The Foreign Ministry spokesman sharply contrasted this disciplined approach with Washington’s long-standing pattern of indiscriminate warfare. “This stands in stark contrast to the United States’ long record of deliberate attacks on civilian targets – schools, hospitals, residential neighborhoods, wedding ceremonies, bridges, and more,” he emphasized.
Highlighting the fundamental divergence in conduct, Baghaei added that there is “a vast difference between a civilized nation that has learned the importance of adhering to moral and humanitarian principles even under the most distressing circumstances, and warmongering rulers who observe no rule of law or ethics in their projection of power.”
These observations arrive as the Islamic Republic continues exercising its legitimate right to self-defense against unprovoked military aggression launched by the United States with Israeli backing. Iranian armed forces have executed precise counter-operations against regional US bases and assets utilized to launch attacks against Iranian territory, including those located in Qatar.
Tehran has continually stressed that its military actions strictly target hostile military objectives and pose zero threat to neighboring countries or their civilian populations. While valuing brotherly relations with Qatar, Tehran maintains its firm resolve to respond to any misuse of Qatari territory or airspace for hostile acts against Iran.
Recent American escalations have involved direct attacks on civilian gatherings within Iran, such as a strike on a wedding ceremony in Sirik—condemned as a war crime reflecting Washington’s ongoing moral degradation. Iranian officials consistently uphold international humanitarian law and Islamic tenets by carefully separating military targets from civilian populations, standing in stark contrast to the documented history of US bombing campaigns targeting civilian infrastructure from Afghanistan to Yemen and now within Iran itself.

The Saba News Agency said in a brief urgent report that the Houthis “targeted a restaurant in the Mokha junction area west of Taiz with a ballistic missile.”

The escalation is among the most significant rounds of fighting in Taiz since the UN-brokered truce in 2022, amid UN warnings over the risk of Yemen sliding back into a wider conflict.
Since September 2014, the Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and other cities, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces control large areas in the south, east, and west of the country.

Vance: US probing airstrike that Iran says hit a wedding party
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 - U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday said the United States is investigating an airstrike that Iran says struck a wedding party in Iran.
"We're investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know," Vance told reporters during a White House press briefing.
"If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran, when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them," Vance added.
Iranian officials say four people died and nearly 70 were wounded by a strike that hit a home during a wedding. Iranian state TV reported on Thursday that a fifth person, a 22-year-old woman, had since died in hospital.

articles.title: U.S. Marine Corps orders 14 more MRADR radar systems
articles.body:
- The Marine Corps awarded Dynetics a $40.8 million modification to build 14 more Medium Range Air Defense Radar systems, with work through August 2028.
- The contract also covers retrofitting four existing MRADR prototypes and four MELPS sensor systems, alongside logistics and software support.
The U.S. Marine Corps has awarded Dynetics a $40.8 million contract modification to build 14 additional Medium Range Air Defense Radar production-representative systems, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The hybrid other transaction agreement modification also funds depot-level technical manual support, program management, engineering change proposals, logistics support and software support. It further requires Dynetics to retrofit four existing MRADR prototype systems and four Marine Expeditionary Long Range Persistent Sensor, or MELPS, systems. Work will be performed primarily in Huntsville, Alabama, accounting for 87.5% of the effort, with the remainder done in Woodlake, California. The contract is expected to be completed by August 2028.
The Marine Corps funded the award with $2,972,730 in fiscal 2025 procurement funds, $31,295,685 in fiscal 2026 procurement funds and $1,500,000 in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds, all obligated at the time of award. The Marine Corps procured the modification under 10 U.S. Code 4022 as a follow-on to an earlier prototype agreement. Marine Corps Systems Command in Quantico, Virginia, is managing the contract.
Dynetics, a Leidos company based in Huntsville, has built the MRADR program since 2023. The Marine Corps first awarded the company a $32 million contract that November to develop four MRADR prototype systems over two years, drawing on sensor work Dynetics had previously done on the MELPS program for the Office of Naval Research. In August 2025, the Marine Corps placed a follow-on order worth roughly $24.9 million for six MRADR production-representative model systems. The new $40.8 million modification adds 14 more of those production-representative units to the program.
MRADR is designed to give Marine units a mobile, 360-degree radar capable of detecting, tracking and identifying aerial threats, including cruise missiles and crewed and uncrewed aircraft. The system relies on digitized antennas, receivers and digital signal processing to build a persistent air picture while producing minimal electromagnetic emissions, a design intended to make the radar harder for adversaries to locate and target.
The Marine Corps intends to integrate MRADR with other ground-based air defense systems already in its inventory, including the AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task-Oriented Radar, known as G/ATOR, and the Medium-Range Intercept Capability system. Together, those systems are meant to give Marine expeditionary units layered detection and engagement capability against helicopters, fixed-wing aircraft, cruise missiles, rockets and drones.

articles.title: IDF raises alert level over concerns of a possible Hamas response to Gaza strikes
articles.body:
Concern is mounting within the IDF Southern Command that commanders in Hamas’s military wing could carry out a guerrilla operation against IDF outposts or patrols along the Yellow Line in response to a series of targeted strikes and the capture of a senior Hamas official earlier this week, sources told Walla on Thursday.
 
Southern Command officials are also not ruling out rocket fire toward Israel as an attempt by Hamas to demonstrate its strength. The sources said the assessment is that Hamas prefers the US not to allow the IDF to conduct deep operations in the strip and therefore may seek to use the period before elections in Israel and the US to respond to recent developments.
Ahead of Rosh Hashanah next weekend, a situational assessment will be held to examine the possibility of a targeted reinforcement of forces in the Gaza Strip. The move could include sending messages to Hamas that any activity against IDF troops or the Israeli home front would lead to an unusual IDF response.
The defense establishment has declined to comment on the arrest of the head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus, but officials said he is a key figure in understanding the organization’s behind-the-scenes activities. According to the officials, his interrogation could help answer critical questions regarding operational plans, protected individuals, methods and tactics, and field commanders who were recently appointed to sensitive positions.
If Gazan forces attack, Israel's response will be severe
On the same day as the arrest, the IDF raised its alert level over concerns of a possible Hamas response. Diplomatic officials conveyed messages through mediators that if Gaza-based forces carried out an attack against IDF soldiers or Israeli civilians following the arrest, Israel’s response would be severe.
The arrest operation was carried out in cooperation with the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and a Gazan Palestinian anti-Hamas militia. IDF and Shin Bet Special Forces entered the al-Shati refugee camp area in the Gaza Strip using vehicles. According to Palestinian reports, Hamas operatives detected the force and a firefight broke out, during which the force was extracted from both the ground and the air. Based on those claims, no arrest was carried out.
However, according to Defense Minister Israel Katz’s statement released after the operation, the arrest did take place. “We do not wait for threats, but rather pursue Hamas terrorists, eliminate them and destroy their terror infrastructure,” he wrote.
Katz said the arrest was carried out in response to an increase in the launching of explosive kites from the Gaza Strip toward Israeli territory. “The response to every launch from Gaza will be powerful and clear. The test will not be in their launches but in our response, and it will be severe,” he emphasized.

articles.title: US, allies want IAEA board to report Iran to UN Security Council, diplomats say
articles.body:
The US and its allies Britain, France and Germany are pushing other countries on the UN nuclear watchdog's board to pass a resolution next week reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, diplomats said on Friday.
If passed, the resolution would follow up on one adopted on June 12 of last year declaring Iran in breach of its non-proliferation obligations for not fully cooperating with an investigation into uranium traces found at undeclared sites.
The US launched an air war against Tehran on February 28 in which, together with Israel, it destroyed or badly damaged Iran's uranium-enrichment facilities.
Iran has not let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors return to the bombed sites since then or verify what remains of its stocks of enriched uranium, some of which was enriched to up to 60% purity, a short step from weapons grade.
Resolution would be culmination of standoff over IAEA's access to nuclear sites
A resolution by the IAEA's 35-nation board reporting Iran to the Security Council would also be the culmination of a standoff over IAEA access to those sites, since the board has passed two resolutions in the past year demanding Iran declare its enriched uranium stocks and grant the IAEA full access to verify them.
A draft text for the resolution has yet to be formally submitted to the board and negotiations between countries over the exact wording are ongoing, diplomats said. A draft is usually formally submitted early in the week of a board meeting.
As a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), Iran has the right to develop nuclear technology, including enrichment, for peaceful purposes. Iran says it would never produce nuclear weapons.
It is, however, the only country to enrich to 60% without making a bomb. The amount it has enriched to that level is "a matter of serious concern" to the IAEA.
The IAEA believes well over 200 kg of that highly enriched uranium has survived the bombardments and is held in a tunnel complex at Isfahan and at the Natanz facility.

articles.body:
The Pentagon instructed US military personnel to stop referring to ongoing operations against Iran as "Operation Epic Fury" in August, CBS reported on Thursday, citing an email sent to the US Air Force.
According to the email, sent on August 7, military leaders were instructed to refer to the conflict as "overseas operations in the CENTCOM AOR [US Central Command Area of Responsibility]," CBS reported.
In response to CBS questioning, the Pentagon stated that Operation Epic Fury had officially ended several months ago, on May 5, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at the White House that the operation had concluded.
"Following the April ceasefire, the administration stated Operation Epic Fury had concluded on May 5," a Defense Department official told CBS. "Subsequent activities have included Freedom of Navigation operations and strikes to further diminish threats posed by the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] to commercial shipping, Gulf countries, and American forces."
The Pentagon did not comment to CBS on why it sent the guidance months after Operation Epic Fury concluded.
Pentagon relabels soldiers killed as 'Overseas Operations Casualties'
The confirmation as to the concluding date of Operation Epic Fury raises questions regarding the status of American soldiers who were killed by Iranian attacks following May 5.
In July, the Pentagon designated four soldiers killed in Jordan and Iraq that month as "Overseas Operations Casualties," separate from the other 14 casualties of Operation Epic Fury listed on its website.
The number of soldiers listed as wounded during Operation Epic Fury also shifted during that time, with 482 soldiers reduced to 417, and an additional 207 soldiers listed as wounded in "Overseas Operations."
At the time, Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell blamed the soldiers' temporary absence on a "a temporary data disruption" on the website in a post on X/Twitter.
"The Department of War is aware of temporary data disruptions on the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) website," he stated. "These site anomalies are currently being resolved in coordination with the Military Services."
CBS contacted a Pentagon official after the recent confirmation that Operation Epic Fury concluded in May. The official said that "Since Operation Epic Fury has concluded, the Department classifies casualties as overseas operations in the CENTCOM area of responsibility."
However, as of Friday, the Defense Department's website continues to list five soldiers wounded in June and one soldier killed in July as casualties of Operation Epic Fury.

articles.title: Shootout between Ukrainian security agencies that injured three under investigation, Zelensky says
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that an investigation would determine what caused a dispute between two of Ukraine's security agencies to escalate into a shootout in Kyiv this week that left three members of the Defense Ministry's HUR Military Intelligence Directorate injured.
The dispute centers on the disappearance for nine days of a Russian nationalist activist fighting alongside Ukrainian troops in the four-and-a-half-year-old war pitting Moscow against Kyiv.
The nationalist said he was detained by the SBU Security Service and obliged to sign a confession that he collaborated with Russian intelligence. He later retracted the statement.
The street clash occurred in central Kyiv on Tuesday after the activist's home in Kyiv was searched. SBU officers fired on members of the HUR unit. The SBU has said it was acting to prevent a Moscow-inspired plot to assassinate Russian anti-Kremlin activists in Kyiv.
"It is important that the truth come out. And that situations like this do not recur," Zelensky said in his nightly video address.
SBU, HUR agencies clash violently over dispute
"An assessment of the heads of these two agencies - the SBU and the HUR - will be made based on the results of an internal investigation. It is completely fair that both sides be brought to account. Both acted precisely in a way that should not have happened," he said.
Two servicemen from the two bodies have been issued notices of suspicion in connection with the incident. Zelensky has dismissed the head of the SBU’s department for the protection of state secrets, Oleh Khramov.

articles.title: Russia Has Been Strapping FPV Drones to Shaheds for a Year, but the Trick Keeps Failing
articles.body:

Russia Has Been Strapping FPV Drones to Shaheds for a Year, but the Trick Keeps Failing
Russia has been experimenting for more than a year with Shahed-type drones as airborne carriers for smaller FPV drones, but the concept has proved unreliable and is rarely used, Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said on September 3.
According to Beskrestnov, Russian forces attach two FPV drones to a conventional Shahed or Gerbera drone, effectively using the larger aircraft to carry the smaller UAVs closer to their intended operating area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The FPV drones are controlled through LTE modems using cellular networks and SIM cards once deployed.
“The effectiveness of this solution is very low, and the enemy uses it rarely—literally once a week or once every two weeks. The FPV often loses connection, control, and crashes,” Beskrestnov explained.
The concept could theoretically extend the operating range of short-range FPV drones by transporting them deep into Ukrainian territory before release. In practice, however, maintaining a reliable cellular connection while the smaller drone is in flight appears to be a significant limitation.
Beskrestnov also pointed to another constraint: the FPV drones can only be carried by conventional propeller-driven Shaheds.
“The FPV drones are attached to an ordinary Shahed. They would simply be blown off a jet-powered one,” he noted.
That distinction has become increasingly important as Russia shifts toward faster jet-powered Shahed variants in strikes against Kyiv, the surrounding region and other Ukrainian cities.
Moscow has increasingly relied on the faster models after Ukraine pushed interception rates against conventional Shahed-type drones above 90%, according to Beskrestnov.
Jet-powered variants are significantly harder to intercept because their higher speed leaves Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and engage them.
Earlier, reports emerged that a Ukrainian remotely operated machine-gun system originally designed for use across multiple combat platforms has now been adapted for aviation, with footage showing the Khyzhak module mounted aboard a helicopter and used to engage Russian Shahed-type drones.

He attributed Iran’s resilience to its religious beliefs, firm determination and experience gained from previous wars, saying these factors had strengthened the country’s ability to withstand the aggression.

articles.title: Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
articles.body:
Repeated attacks on humanitarian warehouses put vital medical aid at risk in Ukraine: WHO
A new airstrike overnight damaged one of the main warehouses used by the World Health Organization (WHO) in Ukraine to store humanitarian medical supplies in the Kyiv region, the UN agency said on Friday.
This is the third attack to affect a WHO-used storage facility in the last three months.
“Yesterday, overnight, between 3 and 4 September, an air attack in Kyiv oblast affected one of WHO's main warehouses, storing humanitarian medical needs and supplies,” said WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier.
Speaking to journalists in Geneva, he explained that “the access to the site remained restricted due to heavy smoke and safety concerns, while assessments of possible damage and stock losses are ongoing.”
No WHO personnel were affected, he said.
Healthcare under fire
This incident follows two other attacks on warehouses used by WHO in different parts of the country in the last three months, with essential medical supplies intended for people living in frontline and hard-to-reach areas.
Two weeks ago, an attack destroyed a WHO humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro, resulting in the loss of half of the medical supplies and equipment intended to support an estimated 225,000 people living in the frontline and hard-to-reach areas, according to the WHO.
“Another warehouse used by WHO in Kyiv oblast was damaged during a large-scale wave of attacks on Kyiv and the region in July,” said Mr. Lindmeier.
Lifeline for civilians
Humanitarian medical supplies are a lifeline for people who need healthcare in frontline and hard-to-reach areas. The WHO spokesperson stressed that attacks on warehouses storing these supplies can delay or disrupt the delivery of essential health support to people who need it most.
The agency is increasingly concerned about the growing pattern of attacks on humanitarian storage facilities nationwide.
“The attacks are part of a broader pattern affecting humanitarian operations across the country. In 2026, at least 20 attacks have affected warehouses storing humanitarian supplies, including 15 attacks on warehouses holding health-related humanitarian supplies,” Mr. Lindmeier said.
He stressed that the locations of United Nations and WHO facilities and warehouses are known to all parties to the conflict as they are communicated through established deconfliction arrangements.
“In my understanding, all warehouses, all UN locations, all WHO locations, are de-conflicted. That means the whereabouts are communicated to all sides of the conflict, and that is well known,” Mr. Lindmeier explained.
Commitment to deliver
Despite the attacks, the WHO continues to work with health partners across Ukraine to ensure that essential medical supplies reach health facilities and communities in need. Following the latest incidents, alternative storage arrangements have already been identified, while efforts are underway to assess the damage and replace lost supplies.
In 2026, the WHO's overall humanitarian response comprised provision of equipment and supplies to over 300 health-care facilities, including primary care centres, hospitals, laboratories, and transit centers, supporting the health system to reach three million beneficiaries.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022, WHO has verified more than 3,000 attacks on healthcare including strikes on health facilities, ambulances, medical supplies and warehouses.

articles.title: Russian Drone Targets Office of Acting SBU Head in Kyiv, Zelenskyy Confirms

Russian Drone Targets Office of Acting SBU Head in Kyiv, Zelenskyy Confirms
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered a “mirrored” retaliatory strike after a Russian drone directly hit the office of acting SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad at the agency’s central Kyiv headquarters on September 4, injuring at least seven people.
Editor’s note: this is a developing story.
A Russian drone directly struck the central headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in Kyiv, specifically targeting the office of acting SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad and causing several casualties, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on September 4.
“Unfortunately, there was a Russian drone strike on the central SBU building on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv opposite St. Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy stated following a conversation with Poklad. He confirmed that emergency personnel had been immediately deployed to the site, noting, “Everyone who was injured will be provided with the necessary assistance.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian president emphasized the deliberate nature of the targeting, stating that “the drone was directed straight into the office of the SBU head in this building.” In response to the attack, Zelenskyy ordered security services to prepare a severe retaliatory strike against Russian targets.
“I gave Poklad the task to respond adequately, tangibly and, if possible, in a mirrored way to the Russians for this strike, when everything is prepared,” Zelenskyy said, concluding that the Ukrainian military “will support this response.”
Kyiv mayor Vitaliy Klitschko stated that there are currently five people injured in the Shevchenkivskyi District. Medical personnel have hospitalized four of the injured.
UPD: The “Zavertaylo” restaurant chain announced on Instagram that one of its locations, located between the SBU Central Administration building and St. Sophia Cathedral in Kyiv, was damaged by an explosion and is currently closed.

articles.title: Norway Seizes Russian Vessel in Arctic Svalbard at Ukraine's Request, Drawing Putin's Fury

Norway Seizes Russian Vessel in Arctic Svalbard at Ukraine's Request, Drawing Putin's Fury
Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the remote Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine's request. The move drew condemnation from the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, who on September 3 compared it to "state terrorism," Associated Press reported.
A Norwegian court ordered the seizure to help Ukraine's state energy company Naftogaz recover a $4.22 billion arbitration award. The award stems from Russia's 2014 illegal annexation of Crimea and its seizure of Ukrainian energy assets, including gas fields and pipelines.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
After Russia refused to pay the 2023 award, Naftogaz began petitioning national courts for orders to seize Russian commercial assets abroad.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, is used for commercial expedition cruises, including to Svalbard. The archipelago lies more than 500 miles (about 800 kilometers) north of the Norwegian mainland and is known for its snow-covered mountains, fjords, and glaciers.
"This is another important step towards restoring justice for Russia's unlawful seizure of Naftogaz assets in Crimea," Naftogaz CEO Sergii Fedorenko stated.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," he added. "We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world."
Putin, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on September 3, criticized the seizure. He also condemned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warning to foreign airlines to avoid Russian airspace because of Ukrainian long-range drone attacks.
Ukraine has pressed a widening financial campaign against Russia in recent months. On August 5, the European Union allocated around $1.6 billion to Kyiv using proceeds from immobilized Russian assets.
Days later, on August 14, Ukraine imposed sanctions on 13 maritime vessels, 11 Russian citizens, and 28 legal entities tied to the removal of grain from occupied territories, with eight of the ships flying the Russian flag.

articles.title: Six Iranian Navy personnel martyred in US strikes in southern Iran
