Six Iranian Navy personnel martyred in US strikes in southern Iran
TEHRAN —Six personnel from the Iranian Navy were killed in US strikes on targets in southern Iran two nights ago, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
The six personnel were identified as: Hossein Mahdavian, Hamed Akati, Amirhossein Salimzadeh, Mohammadreza Baderan, Malek Mousavitabar, Mojtaba Bagheri.
The strikes were part of a broader US military campaign against targets in several parts of Iran. Iranian authorities said the attacks killed both military personnel and civilians, including people who were attending a wedding ceremony in the southern city of Sirik.
Iranian armed forces subsequently launched a series of missile and drone operations against US military positions and bases across the region.

articles.title: Thousands of Lebanese students still displaced by war as school year nears
articles.body:
Thousands of Lebanese students still displaced by war as school year nears
TYRE, Lebanon, Sept 4 - The schoolyard in southern Lebanon echoed with the squeals of playing children despite the beating sun and distant booms of Israeli airstrikes. But for most of the youth there, the public school isn't where they learn. It's where they live.
Thousands of children remain displaced from their hometowns in Lebanon's south six months after a new war erupted between Israel's military and armed group Hezbollah. Many still live in schools-turned-shelters, while others are squeezed into rented apartments with their extended families.
As schools gear up for a new academic year beginning on September 15, families who sought shelter in public schools are wondering where they will go — and how their children can pick up schooling amid so much uncertainty.
Najah Ammar, a grandmother of four school-aged children, hails from the coastal village of Mansouri, but fled Israeli strikes to the public school in the city of Tyre, about 10 km (6 miles) north. About 200 other families now live in the school.
Ammar, 62, has two worries: where she'll live if the school reopens, and how her grandchildren can catch up after losing years of schooling during repeated conflicts between Israel and Hezbollah since 2023.
"They’ve been out of school for two years — the last war and this war. My son’s daughter, the poor girl is eight years old. She was a second year and she’s still a second year," said Ammar.
DISPLACED FEAR COSTS OF NEW SCHOOL YEAR
Since March 2, Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon, including more than 250 children, and wounded another 12,000, including 1,000 children, according to Lebanon's health ministry.
At the fighting's peak, more than one million people — nearly a quarter of the population — were displaced. Most have returned home but more than 340,000 remain displaced, because their hometowns are destroyed or fall within territory occupied by Israel's military.
Rula al-Awad, a 27-year-old mother of two also displaced from Mansouri, said she lacked the education to help her daughter through online classes, but brings her pen and paper so she can at least keep writing.
Awad is staying in an apartment but brings her two children to the Tyre school to play and wants to enroll them for the new year. Yet she fears she won't be able to afford schoolbooks or uniforms.
"I hope we can look ahead to a future that is beautiful for the kids – then we can consider having hope, so that when we tell our kids that things are beautiful, they believe us instead of feeling that we're lying to them," she said.
Zeinab Moussa, 56, who lives in tents in the school hall with her sons and grandchildren, says the children can only snatch brief moments of happiness.
"An NGO will come, they play a little bit. The NGO goes away, they despise everything," she said. "I just wish that the children could live their childhoods. But there’s no childhood now."
DOZENS OF LEBANESE SCHOOLS DAMAGED, DESTROYED
Out of nearly 80 public schools still used as shelters as the school year approached, almost half have been emptied and will reopen as schools, Lebanon's education ministry told Reuters. About 30 will partially reopen while continuing to serve as shelters, leaving nine schools still fully used as shelters.
Another 50 Lebanese public schools have been destroyed or severely damaged in the war, and more than 200 others have suffered moderate or minor damage, the ministry said. The United Nations said the impact on schools would jeopardize the new school year for at least 100,000 children.
Last month, the Lebanese army said Israeli troops had blown up a public school and a kindergarten in the southern village of Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters questions on the school.
Lebanon's Education Minister Rima Karami said this week she aimed to ensure as many students as possible from the south could continue their education, whether in their hometowns, if safe, or in displacement.
Save the Children, which is supporting the Tyre school, said only a durable ceasefire could resolve the crisis.
"Children we spoke to over the past few days know what the solution is. It's a political solution. There's no humanitarian solution here," said Danny Glenwright, president of Save the Children Canada. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Strikes Abandoned Soviet-Era Planes in Kyiv to Send a Signal to the US, Lawmaker Says
articles.body:

Russia Strikes Abandoned Soviet-Era Planes in Kyiv to Send a Signal to the US, Lawmaker Says
Russia may have struck two long-inactive Yak-40 passenger aircraft at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv International Airport (Zhuliany) on September 4, according to preliminary information relayed by Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksii Honcharenko.
Honcharenko, a member of Ukraine's parliament, reported the strike in a Telegram post, describing the target as unusually obsolete. Kyiv Post, which relayed his account, emphasized that no official confirmation of the reported attack had been issued.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Honcharenko framed the incident as a deliberate message from Russian leader Vladimir Putin to Washington.
"Essentially, Putin is sending a signal to the Americans: I don't want to negotiate and I won't," he wrote, questioning the purpose of what he called a demonstrative strike.
The two aircraft were Soviet-era passenger jets that, according to Honcharenko, had not flown even before the full-scale invasion began. He indicated the planes had sat out of service for years, making them a target of negligible military value. As of his post, both the damage and the strike itself remained preliminary and unverified.
Zhuliany is a civilian airport in the Ukrainian capital that handled passenger flights before the full-scale Russian invasion.
Ukraine closed its airspace to civilian aviation on February 24, 2022, and it remains closed because of the risks posed by the war.
As a result, regular passenger flights do not operate to Kyiv, and Ukrainians, foreign visitors, and official delegations generally enter and travel around the country by train or road, often crossing through neighboring European states.
Honcharenko tied the timing to an anticipated visit by US representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, whom he stated were due in Kyiv on Sunday after a Saturday stop in Moscow.
He noted the envoys had been close to agreeing to fly into Boryspil Airport, but the strike had likely pushed them toward reaching the capital by road instead.
The prospect of an envoy visit has been trailed by repeated postponements for months, with the American mission promised and delayed several times over the summer. Ukrainian officials had earlier assessed that Putin held little genuine interest in negotiations, an evaluation the reported strike appeared to reinforce.

articles.title: Iraq proposes new 6+2 Gulf security framework
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
6+2: An Iraqi vision for a new regional security formula
Despite several senior Iraqi officials in Baghdad repeatedly promoting the vision of "joint Gulf security" in recent weeks, there has been no response from outside Iraq.
The vision, known as 6+2 and referring to the six Gulf Cooperation Council states alongside Iraq and Iran, was unveiled by Iraqi government security adviser Qasim Al-Araji last week. The plan calls for a Gulf security system based on "respect for the sovereignty of states".
He said the 6+2 initiative aims to "address the crisis of confidence" between the Arab Gulf states and Iran, without providing further details about its content.
In remarks carried by Iraqi state television, he said: "From this standpoint, Iraq affirms its responsibility to consolidate state sovereignty and the independence of its decisions, place weapons and decisions on war and peace in its hands, prevent its territory from being used to threaten neighbouring countries, and pursue a balanced foreign policy that contributes to de-escalation and the containment of crises."
The Iraqi government has not officially adopted the initiative, nor has it issued a document outlining its provisions.
Political sources in Baghdad said it was proposed last month at a meeting of the ruling Coordination Framework coalition at the beginning of August, attended by Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, as an Iraqi initiative to establish security understandings with the Gulf states and Iran.
However, a key problem with the initiative may explain the lack of response.
It focuses on the commitment of the eight states bordering the Arabian Gulf not to use their territory to attack other countries. This corresponds with the Iranian narrative repeatedly used after each attack on the Arab Gulf states: that Iran does not target the Gulf states but rather US bases located in their territory and used to attack Iran.
The Gulf states, as well as Jordan, naturally reject this claim, while Tehran has provided no evidence for its allegations.
A senior Iraqi parliamentarian in Baghdad from the Reconstruction and Development bloc, one of the components of the ruling Coordination Framework coalition, said the Iraqi initiative is based on the principle of neutrality in the current war against Iran, which the United States has been waging against it for many months, according to him.
He revealed that the initiative has been accepted by leaders of the ruling coalition but naturally "lacks a guarantor" to make any agreement sustainable and ensure compliance with it, particularly by the Iranians.
The lawmaker, who asked not to be named, added that the Iraqi initiative or vision had received no response from the six Gulf states.
However, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed any initiative aimed at easing the current tensions.
On Wednesday, Al-Araji returned to present the same initiative, saying that "6+2 Gulf security", which includes Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman, alongside Iraq and Iran, is based on the principle of "not using the territory of any state to threaten neighbouring states".
He stressed that his country is capable of "preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a launching point for attacks against neighbouring countries".
Through the initiative, Baghdad aims to once again present Iraq as a bridge for dialogue between Iran and the Gulf states, according to Iraqi security affairs expert Ahmed Al-Nuaimi.
He explained that the initiative was presented through communication channels between Iraq and several Gulf states but did not receive the expected response.
He attributed this to several reasons, most notably that the initiative is based on the principle of states not attacking one another from their own territory.
Gulf states consider this a misleading Iranian narrative designed to cover up repeated attacks against them under the pretext of targeting US bases.
Iranian attacks have hit ports, airports, oil facilities and even civilian sites in the Gulf states, resulting in deaths and injuries, and were not limited to those bases.
Iraq itself has also become a launch point for attacks carried out by armed groups allied with Iran.
However, Al-Nuaimi pointed out that the most important aspect of this vision, which appears to be supported by figures allied with Iran inside Iraq, is that it is a political position directed against the United States.
None of the Gulf states wants to depart from their relatively stable position in this war, which is to remain on the sidelines and avoid being drawn into the war or aligning with either side.
What Iraq has announced so far remains unclear.
No official document containing the initiative's points or principles has been disclosed, and the Foreign Ministry has yet to take any action on it, according to Kurdish Iraqi politician Ali Shankali.
Shankali told The New Arab that Iraq itself still faces problems transporting its oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as repeated attacks on Erbil and Sulaymaniyah carried out by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from time to time against US interests or Kurdish groups opposed to Tehran.
Iran is also strengthening the position of Iraqi armed factions that refuse to cooperate with the Iraqi state in handing over their weapons, making any initiatives, even if other countries take an interest in them, "unlikely to be guaranteed in implementation".
This is not the first time Iraq has proposed the same initiative.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in late June that his country had proposed holding an eight-party meeting bringing together the Gulf Cooperation Council states, Iraq and Iran to discuss security in the Gulf region.
Hussein said at a joint press conference with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in Baghdad that "the security of the region should be the responsibility of its states, and different frameworks could be established to protect those states".
He affirmed Iraq's readiness to host such a meeting to discuss the issue, as well as economic relations between the countries of the region.
The Iranian foreign minister welcomed the Iraqi proposal at the press conference, saying, "The issue of security in the Gulf region should be reconsidered, and a new framework should be established that includes all the countries of the region without interference from any country from outside it."
Former Iraqi parliamentarian Mohammed Al-Daraji said that many visions and initiatives had been proposed recently within the Iraqi political scene, but they did not go beyond being matters for domestic discussion and had no bearing on the conflict or the political and security calculations in the region.
Al-Daraji explained that Iraq's ability to play any positive security role in the region would remain "dependent on the government's ability to control armed groups and prevent them from using Iraqi territory to target other countries, such as Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait".
He said the absence of a Gulf position on the Iraqi vision may be because it had not formally reached them or because they see it as an attempt to make them party to a crisis at a time when they are in fact parties adversely affected by the war in terms of security, economics and politics and were not responsible for it.

articles.title: Ukraine’s FPV Drones Burn Rare Russian 2S43 Malva, One of Moscow’s Newest Howitzers, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s FPV Drones Burn Rare Russian 2S43 Malva, One of Moscow’s Newest Howitzers, Video
Ukrainian FPV drone operators destroyed a Russian 2S43 Malva, one of Moscow’s relatively rare new wheeled self-propelled howitzers, the 22nd Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on September 4.
Ukrainian reconnaissance first located the Russian artillery system before FPV crews were directed toward the target. Several drones subsequently struck the Malva, destroying the vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The 2S43 Malva is a 152mm self-propelled howitzer mounted on an 8×8 wheeled chassis. Russia began serial deliveries of the system to its military in late 2023, introducing it as a more mobile alternative to heavier tracked artillery.
At around 32 metric tons, the Malva can reach speeds of approximately 50 mph and travel up to roughly 620 miles without refueling. It carries a five-person crew and up to 30 artillery rounds.
Its primary weapon is the 152mm 2A64 gun, the same type used by Russia’s tracked 2S19 Msta-S self-propelled howitzer. With standard ammunition, the gun has an effective range of roughly 15 miles.
The wheeled chassis allows the Malva to move between firing positions more quickly than many traditional tracked artillery systems, an increasingly important capability on a battlefield where drones can locate artillery shortly after it opens fire.
But the system remains relatively scarce. Open-source estimates indicate that only a few dozen Malvas have entered Russian service, making each confirmed loss particularly notable as Moscow continues introducing the relatively new platform.
Ukrainian units have previously targeted Malvas with drones, gradually adding the system to the growing list of modern Russian artillery vulnerable to FPV strikes.
The 22nd Brigade marked the latest loss with a play on the howitzer’s floral name.
“The ‘Malvas’ by the house will bloom no more,” the brigade said.
Previously, Ukrainian FPV drone operators from the MARA Unmanned Systems Battalion destroyed what the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade described as possibly one of the last Russian infantry fighting vehicles remaining in its area of responsibility on the Lyman front.

articles.title: Teva Ukraine warehouse hit twice in Russian attack, raising supply concerns
articles.body:
A Russian attack struck a warehouse operated by pharmaceutical giant Teva in Ukraine twice on Friday, the company said, damaging part of the infrastructure used to support the country's medicine supply chain.
No employees were injured, according to Teva Ukraine. The company said all of its workers were safe and that it was providing support to employees directly affected by the attack.
The strike comes as Russia continues its war against Ukraine, with critical civilian infrastructure repeatedly coming under attack. For Ukrainians who rely on daily medications, damage to pharmaceutical facilities can create another layer of uncertainty in a country already operating under wartime conditions.
Teva says it is working to keep medicines available
Teva Ukraine said it continues to operate while assessing the damage caused by the attack. The company emphasized that millions of people depend on its medicines and that for many patients, regular treatment is not something that can simply be put on hold.
Teva said it is taking steps to minimize any impact on medicine supplies and keep needed medications available to Ukrainian patients. The company has not reported an immediate shortage or interruption in medicine deliveries as a result of the attack. However, it is still evaluating the damage and the potential effect on its distribution operations.
A major pharmaceutical presence in Ukraine
Teva Ukraine is the Ukrainian operation of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, an Israeli-founded pharmaceutical company headquartered in Tel Aviv. It has a major international presence and serves patients in countries around the world.
The company is among the three largest pharmaceutical companies in Ukraine. It employs more than 350 people and produces or supplies more than 250 generic and original medicines.
Another pharmaceutical facility hit in Kyiv region
The Teva warehouse was not the only pharmaceutical facility affected by a Russian attack this week.
According to Ukrainian media, on Thursday, a pharmaceutical complex operated by Biocon in the Kyiv region caught fire following a Russian attack. The facility, located in the Boryspil district, is one of Ukraine's largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouses.
The company said it is doing everything possible to limit the attack's impact and ensure Ukrainian patients continue to receive the medications they need.

articles.title: SBI denies reports of alleged disclosure of SSU personnel data to Russia
articles.body:
SBI denies reports of alleged disclosure of SSU personnel data to Russia
According to Ukrinform, the SBI reported this.
The SBI said it had not provided representatives of the Russian side with any data concerning employees of Ukraine’s intelligence and security services.
It also said that reports claiming that SBI Director Oleksii Sukhachov had allegedly instructed bureau employees to hand over such data to Russia were untrue.
“The dissemination of unsubstantiated and inaccurate allegations is a deliberate attempt to discredit the SBI and, directly, its leadership,” the bureau stressed.
The SBI emphasized that any information made available to its employees in the course of their official duties is used exclusively in accordance with the law and within the framework of specific criminal proceedings.
At the same time, information concerning the dissemination of personal data belonging to law enforcement officers has been entered into the Unified Register of Pretrial Investigations, and a pretrial investigation has been launched.
Law enforcement officers are establishing the source from which the information was obtained and disseminated, as well as all the circumstances surrounding its publication.
The SBI stressed that any attempts to use the personal data of Ukrainian law enforcement officers to discredit them, threaten their security, or pass the information on to third parties will receive an appropriate legal assessment.
According to media reports, posts appeared on social media claiming that the SBI had passed the data of three SSU counterintelligence officers to Ihor Mosiichuk, a pro-Russian former member of parliament.
As Ukrinform reported, SBI employees have launched a pretrial investigation into the circumstances of a conflict between SSU personnel and servicemen of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU). Two individuals have been served with notices of suspicion in the criminal proceedings.

articles.title: Finance Minister Marchenko warned of Ukraine’s most difficult budget situation since the start of the war ahead of a "very difficult winter" - media
articles.body:
Finance Minister Marchenko warned of Ukraine’s most difficult budget situation since the start of the war ahead of a "very difficult winter" - media
Kyiv • UNN
The Finance Minister forecasts a budget deficit of up to $32.6 billion and a possible postponement of non-military payments. He called on the EU to use Russian assets.
Ukraine’s Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko warned of possible liquidity problems in the state budget and delays in some non-military payments due to rising defense spending. He also called on EU countries to consider a new Ukrainian plan for using frozen Russian assets. Marchenko made the statement in an interview with Euronews, UNN writes.
Details
Ukraine’s finance minister warned that the country may have to cut non-military spending if it is unable to secure funding from its allies. He urged European ministers to "think outside the box" as Kyiv prepares for another winter of Russian escalation.
Serhii Marchenko, who has been responsible for the country’s finances since 2020, told Euronews that Ukraine had not faced such a difficult budgetary situation since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Because of the focus on military spending and weapons procurement, other budget items may suffer, and payments may be delayed if a solution is not found.
We are already seeing some liquidity problems and anticipating a certain shortfall of funds in our budget. This means that due to the lack of liquidity, we may have to postpone some payments unrelated to the war. The consequences will be
Asked whether this could affect external creditors, Marchenko answered that it would not.
At the same time, he said, the consequences may be felt at the local level, particularly with regard to the construction of shelters and infrastructure, which he called "still important," as the country prepares for another winter of Russian attacks.
"We have not faced such a situation since 2022; back then, we really suffered greatly from a lack of liquidity. Now we are again dangerously approaching the same scenario we faced in 2022."
He also reported that the intensity of Russian attacks on Ukraine increased sharply in August. Marchenko said he was working on a new budget based on the assumption that the war would continue into 2027. In his assessment, a funding gap of $32.6 billion would need to be covered. According to him, the IMF, whose representatives visited Kyiv this week, cites similar figures.
The war has escalated very rapidly. We are fully aware of this ourselves. Compared with last month, it is a completely different reality, given the recent attacks on our logistics. We expect a very difficult winter. Escalation means that we need to find the resources to get through it
"Think outside the box"
Ukraine’s finance minister urged European ministers to take a creative approach to finding solutions and consider a new Ukrainian plan to use approximately $300 billion in frozen Russian assets.
Last December, the plan was rejected by EU ministers, who were unable to overcome differences among the member states. Instead, they decided on joint financing for a €90 billion loan.
Last week, a group of EU countries led by Sweden revived the proposal, arguing that the costs of the war effort should be fairly distributed among European taxpayers. Since President Donald Trump took office, the EU has largely been left alone to finance this support.
Marchenko welcomed the move and said he hoped more countries would join the initiative by the scheduled September meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
According to him, the new Ukrainian plan, which provides for the transfer of responsibility for the assets currently held in Belgium, contains "entirely new elements" intended to reduce the legal risks for the Belgian government and Euroclear, where the assets are held.
"We want to discuss this; the plan creates new conditions under which Belgium will not be responsible for legal disputes with Russia, but this will be the shared responsibility of all 27 countries."
However, Ukraine and its allies supporting the plan, including neighboring Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain, are facing significant difficulties in trying to revive the idea.
Last December, amid serious concerns from the European Central Bank and strong resistance from key member states — Italy and France — the EU postponed lengthy negotiations on the use of frozen assets.
The reasons cited included concerns about possible retaliatory measures by Russia, reputational damage to the eurozone, and lengthy legal disputes related to possible lawsuits by Moscow over the confiscation of assets.

articles.title: Rare repair job finished on U.S. nuclear missile system
articles.body:
- The 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron completed its first full removal, refurbishment and reinstallation of a Minuteman III suspension system on August 18 near Minot Air Force Base.
- The all-civilian squadron employs 196 people across five bases and is the only Department of War unit authorized for depot-level Minuteman III maintenance.
Air Force maintenance crews completed a first-of-its-kind overhaul of a Minuteman III missile suspension system on August 18, removing the component from a launch facility near Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, shipping it to California for a full refurbishment, and reinstalling it back at the same site.
The work was carried out by the 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron, a unit better known by its historical name, Rivet MILE, short for Minuteman Integrated Life Extension. The squadron handles depot-level maintenance across the Air Force’s fleet of Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, the land-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad.
“The suspension system that was removed from one of the launch facilities earlier this year was the first operation site at Minot AFB to be removed, transported to Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, refurbished and returned to be reinstalled,” said Roy Ring, 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron production superintendent.
Inside a Minuteman III launch facility, the suspension system helps hold and protect the missile within its silo. Routine upkeep on the system is normally handled on-site through preventative maintenance rather than by removing and rebuilding the entire assembly. A complete overhaul, like the one just finished, happens rarely across the Minuteman III fleet.
“The complete overhaul of a suspension system does not happen often across the Minuteman III fleet,” Ring said. “Since the creation of the Depot Maintenance Teams in the mid-1980s, known as Rivet Mile and now the 583rd Missile Maintenance Squadron, mechanics have been routinely inspecting and repairing the suspension systems.”
The squadron is the only one in the Department of War authorized to perform this level of maintenance on Minuteman III facilities, both underground and above ground, according to KyAnn Betz, the squadron’s director.
“We have a full maintenance shop at each missile wing for local manufacturing and repair,” Betz said. “We also assist with field-level maintenance if needed.”
Unlike most Air Force squadrons, the 583rd has no active-duty service members. It is staffed entirely by civilian employees, with more than 250 combined years of Minuteman III experience at each base where it operates. The squadron employs 196 people across five separate units at Minot Air Force Base, Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, and Hill Air Force Base in Utah.
The Air Force has operated the Minuteman III since 1971, and roughly 400 of the missiles remain deployed at bases in North Dakota, Montana and Wyoming. The squadron’s approach traces back to a Minuteman maintenance and service-life program the Air Force launched in 1985, which formed the basis for what eventually became the 583rd.
By completing the full removal, refurbishment and reinstallation cycle at an operational site, the squadron demonstrated that major structural components of the missile system can be taken off-site for a complete rebuild rather than repaired in place. The Air Force has not said whether it plans to repeat this approach at other launch facilities or how often future full suspension system overhauls might occur.
